17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Select the correct options below regarding the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.

$\,$
The $x$-axis is a {{field-1}} line.

$\,$
The $y$-axis is a {{field-2}} line.

$\,$
The equilibrium point (origin) is {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{-t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis and approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\text{stable}$ line.

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ with the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis and move away from the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\text{unstable}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\text{a saddle point}.$

Which of the following curves is simple, closed, and negatively oriented?" :question/worked-solution "A simple closed curve is positively oriented if, when traveling along it, one always has the curve interior to the left and the curve exterior to the right. Otherwise, the curve is negatively oriented.

A curve is positively oriented if it is traversed counterclockwise and is negatively oriented if it is traversed clockwise.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the curves:

- Curve I is negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed clockwise.

- Curve II is not negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed counterclockwise, so it is positively oriented.

- Curve III is not negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed counterclockwise, so it is positively oriented.

- Curve IV is negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed clockwise.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and IV only.""} {:db/id 17592186362289 :question/id #uuid "e90b8b78-8fe2-56fc-abef-7b6866f9bd17" :question/math-academy-id "q-98336"} {:db/id 17592186362290 Otherwise, the curve is negatively oriented. 

A curve is positively oriented if it is traversed counterclockwise and is negatively oriented if it is traversed clockwise.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the curves:

- Curve I is neither simple nor closed.

- Curve II is a simple and closed curve but it is not negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed counterclockwise, so it is positively oriented.

- Curve III is simple, closed, negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed clockwise.

- Curve IV is simple, closed, negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed clockwise.

17592186045486} :question/problem "$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\text{__________},\,z⟩
$$

The vector-valued function $r(z,\theta )$ above parametrizes the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $x=\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}$ by  $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [1,5].$ What is the second  component of $r?$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d3/d3302b5f4ea4c0387d70ac8f78e03e486fff9579f1a6b5e5cec08a31cde76af3.png)

 

A point $(x,y,z)$ on the surface generated by rotating the graph of $x=f(z)$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis has the position vector

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [a,b],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

First, notice that $x=f(z)=\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,5].$   

So, the parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
r(z,\theta )=⟨\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,z\in [1,5],\,\theta \in [0,2\pi ).
$$

Therefore, the second component of $r$ is $\sqrt{{z}^{2}-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$"} {:db/id 17592186172132 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171712 :question/id #uuid ⟨\text{_______}\,,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩
$$

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis for $x\in [0,\pi ]$ is given above. What is the $1$st component of the product?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\ge 0$ for all $x\in [0,\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨x,f(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(x,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ and

$$
D={(x,\theta )\,:\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂x},\,\frac{∂y}{∂x},\,\frac{∂z}{∂x}⟩=⟨1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨0,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f{f}^{′},\,-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172379 :question/id #uuid "5660a1ea-1c96-5f39-8bde-a992c1f8c03a" :question/math-academy-id "q-161069"} {:db/id 17592186278362 :question/id #uuid ⟨\,\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,,\,\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,,\,\text{_______}⟩
$$

 

The fundamental vector product of the surface of revolution generated by rotating the curve $y=\sqrt{z-1}$ by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [1,10]$ is given above. What is the $3$rd component of the product?" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $y=\sqrt{z-1}\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,10].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is  

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=\sqrt{z-1},$ and  

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,1\le z\le 10,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\sqrt{z-1},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z-1}}.$ So, finally, we conclude that the fundamental vector product is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}=⟨\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\sqrt{z-1}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186172133 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171713 :question/id #uuid "a2ff0c76-0d26-51a2-a2fb-498ff5f85559" :question/math-academy-id "e-12365"} :knowledge-point/id $x={z}^{4}+1$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $z$-axis for $z\in [-1,1].$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $x={z}^{4}+1\ge 0$ for all $z\in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=1+{z}^{4},$ and

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,-1\le z\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(z)=1+{z}^{4},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(z)=4{z}^{3}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{z}^{4})\sqrt{1+(4{z}^{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{z}^{4})\sqrt{1+16{z}^{6}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186371948 :question/id #uuid "1297d2b2-529f-5b54-8024-028cb62e9052" :question/math-academy-id "q-161098" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186172133 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "Notice that $y=\operatorname{ln}⁡z\ge 0$ for all $z\in [1,e].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(z)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,f(z)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,z⟩,\,(z,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡z,$ and

$$
D={(z,\theta )\,:\,1\le z\le e,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂z},\,\frac{∂y}{∂z},\,\frac{∂z}{∂z}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{f}^{′}f{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,{f}^{′}f⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(-f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+({f}^{′}f)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=\operatorname{ln}⁡z,$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=\frac{1}{z}.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\operatorname{ln}⁡z\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{z})}^{2}}\,\text{d}z \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{e}\operatorname{ln}⁡z\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389126 :question/id #uuid "0abbafda-b663-58bc-a5e8-afa7f578ba96" :question/math-academy-id "q-161091"} {:db/id 17592186415537 :question/id #uuid the $y$-axis for $y\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2})\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-\pi ,\pi ].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2}),$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-\pi \le y\le \pi ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2}),$ we obtain ${f}^{′}(y)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2}).$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2})\sqrt{1+{(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{y}{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{y}{2})\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{y}{2})}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048972 :topic/id #uuid "d04b4eec-dbc6-5996-ac55-c66543b6de53" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186172134 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171716 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y,z)=x-2y-2z$ on the intersection of the plane $x+y+z=2$ and the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=x-2y-2z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x+y+z=2,\,h(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=2 \\ h(x,y,z)=1\end{aligned}
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda +2\mu x \\ -2=\lambda  \\ -2=\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{3}{2\mu } \\ \lambda =-2 \\ \mu z=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the third equation above, we must have $z=0.$

Next, we substitute $z=0$  into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=1$ and $z=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ 1+y+0 & =2 \\ 1+y & =2 \\ y & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-1$ and $z=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+z & =2 \\ -1+y+0 & =2 \\ -1+y & =2 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(1,1,0),\,(-1,3,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(1,1,0)$ | $(-1,3,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $-1$ | $-7$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-1,3,0),$ and its  minimum value is $-7.$"} {:db/id 17592186172135 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186171717 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle." :question/worked-solution "![](images/d4/d4e5b78932f8ff6155ac81e12538eb31ac211c9d27d6a2b0c67542527ccd3b2a.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4-x & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=4\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=4\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (4-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =4(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+18 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-{x}^{2}+36 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(4)=\sqrt{-(4)^{2}+8(4)+36}=2\sqrt{13}\,m/s
$$"} {:db/id 17592186365260 :question/id #uuid "6e8a8914-09f4-5fec-89f5-6922293a4aaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-163549"} {:db/id 17592186365281 :question/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/de/dea7eed9213ddf1bb3293950e2490b120a061e9add1172d3b850ccbc58f90454.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(y+x)\,i+x\,j$ and $C$ is the arc of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=4$ traversed from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we need to parameterize the curve. Notice that we can write its equation as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, our curve is a part-ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $2$ and $1$ respectively. This curve can be parameterized as

$$
r(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

So, along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =(y+x)\,i+x\,j \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2(-{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F(r)\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,dt \\  & =[\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =[-1+0]-[1-0] \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186345268 :question/id #uuid "1c70d6fc-ab49-5aab-b1d0-4a65a7ea2b5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-77032"} {:db/id 17592186345269 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/de/de3e018fa1382ee2250d1b2e256e3b47cafef346852007f0e6afb84342d7cb04.png)

Consider the vector field $F=3x\,i-2y\,j$ and a rectangle $C$ with base $4$ and height $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown above. Calculate the flux of $F$ across $C.$

*Hint: You may use the fact that, due to symmetry, the flux is equal across the vertical sides, and similarly for the horizontal sides.*" :question/worked-solution "If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](images/09/0950c559d5d6df93cf40afd8fdbd07f090f864fa462083bfd496246e7f2bded9.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-3,3].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =3{\int }_{-3}^{3}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{-3}^{3}\text{d}t \\  & =6\cdot 6 \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=36.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+3j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}3\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-6)\cdot 4 \\  & =-24.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-24.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot 36+2\cdot (-24)=24.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050793} {:db/id 17592186049617 :topic/id #uuid "04ff54ad-5d9d-5751-8a07-6602f0f05410" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186179765 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $F(x,y)=2xi-2y\,j$ over the domain $D={R}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "The streamlines of a vector field are the level curves of its stream function and are tangential to the vector field at every point. 

If $F$ represents the velocity field of a fluid flow, then they show the path traced out by a massless particle as it moves with the flow.

A vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ with a simply connected domain $D⊆{R}^{2}$ has a stream function $ψ(x,y)$ if and only if

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

Note that 

$$
F(x,y)=2xi-2y\,j
$$

 is a vector field with simply connected domain $D,$ where $P(x,y)=2x$ and $Q(x,y)=-2y.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $F$ has a stream function, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2-2=0.
$$

Next, we find a stream function. A function $ψ(x,y)$ is a stream function of the vector field $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ if 

$$
P=\frac{∂ψ}{∂y},\,Q=-\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\frac{∂ψ}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂ψ}{∂x}=2y.
$$

Integrating these equations, we obtain the following:

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy+f(x),\,ψ(x,y)=2xy+g(y)
$$

where $f$ and $g$ are arbitrary functions. Finally, setting $f=g=0,$ we have

$$
ψ(x,y)=2xy.
$$

Finally, we find the level curves of the stream function $ψ(x,y)=2xy$ given by the equations $ψ(x,y)=c.$

Notice that the range of $ψ(x,y)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, we will consider level curves for any value of $c.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}ψ(x,y) & =c \\ 2xy & =c \\ y & =\frac{c}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above gives us a family of hyperbolas with asymptotes $y=0$ and $x=0$ and, for $c=0,$ the lines $y=0$ and $x=0.$ Therefore, the correct graph (along with the vector field $F$) is as follows:

values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$ 

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

:question/worked-solution "We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ,\,y=1.
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta }=0.
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(0)}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{0}{-{csc}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186188282 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186187986 :question/id #uuid "deaef5cc-99fb-57e5-a6f2-22f17a7f00af" :question/math-academy-id "e-10033"} :knowledge-point/id Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are discrete random variables. Find $\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2]$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above and the corresponding conditional expected value is ${\mu }_{X|2}=8.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional variance of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=y] & =\text{E}[(X-{\mu }_{X|y})^{2}\,|\,Y=y] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}\,|\,Y=y]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2} \\  & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)]-{\mu }_{X|y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order to find ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ let's first find the marginal distribution of $Y,$ corresponding to the column totals: 

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=5$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ |
| $X=10$ | $\frac{2}{9}$ | $\frac{1}{3}$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $\frac{4}{9}$ | $\frac{5}{9}$ |

The conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$ is

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)}.
$$

Therefore, dividing each joint probability by the corresponding column total, we obtain the conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y:$

| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=5$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{2}{5}$ |
| $X=10$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{3}{5}$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ |

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X\,|\,Y=2] & =[{\sum }_{x}{x}^{2}\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,2)]-{\mu }_{X|2}^{2} \\  & =[{5}^{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}+{10}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{5}]-{8}^{2} \\  & =10+60-64 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Compute $P(X>2)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}},\, & x\ge 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>2) & =P(2<X<\infty ) \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{x+1}]}_{2}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262580 :question/id #uuid "8ea64e3a-0876-5727-96dc-6cee351571a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-126032"} {:db/id 17592186354555 :question/id #uuid 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "![](images/9a/9a66f9263c9009f634668e826f0a84320103589b9c270360d7b2465c71e74592.png)

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}2xz\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the top one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*" :question/worked-solution "![](images/49/49a3333a52a6b7d7451095dbc46ab1009df491c92726436929a6f93cff38db60.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type I region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,y)\in D,\,\,0\le z\le 3-2x},
$$

where

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](images/df/dfa0a80bc323401f050d1302dc42c92558d8b566d9b0f985e955d34eb5cc15bd.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 3-2x}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2xz\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz\,dy\,dx.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $x$ and $y$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{3-2x}2xz\,dz]dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}[x{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=3-2x}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}x(3-2x)^{2}\,dy\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3}){[y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2(9x-12{x}^{2}+4{x}^{3})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(18x-24{x}^{2}+8{x}^{3})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$

17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Change the order of integration in the integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ and then $z.$" :question/worked-solution "We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(z),$ ${v}_{2}(z),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(z)}^{{v}_{2}(z)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type II region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type II region, we first sketch the projection onto the $yz$-plane, given by

$$
E={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4},\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

as shown below.

![](images/e3/e32a019900b77c0bb84b4599b8899e3d0d32ae07d9674da126db34394b97ea24.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where $0\le x\le \operatorname{tan}⁡y.$

![](images/af/af629672ff2fd31eeae585ad4941fb8682941444cd34383392fb0a6bec24396e.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type II *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](images/04/04dc917237ab002263e35fb4a84c264fef240fefaa456c5249d6e24d0c8ebe28.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x,z),$ is

$$
x=\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,⟹\,y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x.
$$

- The right boundary of the region is

$$
y=\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\le y\le \frac{\pi }{4}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/b2/b2a6fc02441bb6013b6f54d49ceefafc1468b291ae4149847290135bbf2d2e56.png)

We now consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by 

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=1.
$$

![](images/b9/b942dbfba8276421620df6258c9951c2b91a5d2dea18c84260c90b6cbe6f760b.png)

Hence, we have that

$$
D={(x,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $x,$ then $z,$ we obtain

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{tan}⁡y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\operatorname{arctan}⁡x}^{\pi /4}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}z.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281479 :question/id #uuid "4f5b1d02-5004-52a1-b833-f3c606e282e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-162482"} {:db/id 17592186281482 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198562 :question/id #uuid "48e09a9b-efe0-5a6d-96f4-c82dbcd33806" :question/math-academy-id "q-138095" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1512bf0f-a0b6-5737-8456-15bf7348d13a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414668} {:answer/id #uuid "189d044b-20ef-594f-9050-30d36ea1c805" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414669} {:answer/id #uuid "3cba96ef-b9b9-582c-9ce3-fb19b45e7859" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414670} {:answer/id #uuid "b75669b6-5915-5577-8d99-85ede9b169dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414671} {:answer/id #uuid "e53e0f0c-01ad-5114-93c5-0442b0a0663a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186414672}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414668} :answer-field/id #uuid "72e392f4-71c8-5797-8085-77f0d25ff7b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414673}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $3.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186389636 :question/id #uuid "2f869ed0-df60-5562-b5c5-b1ddb2293f45" :question/math-academy-id "q-170504"} {:db/id 17592186410196 :question/id #uuid "5e6637da-fa52-5317-a60a-ab7680b44bc0" :question/math-academy-id "q-138128" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1700f9a6-fd4f-55e6-a5b2-c7c162c8b09c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410167} {:answer/id #uuid "56db98f5-8954-5a74-9db5-ea9ad36d4145" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410174} {:answer/id #uuid "5fd6a7be-2123-5e1c-93b5-fa6a69ebca48" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410178} {:answer/id #uuid "6f32c544-2ebd-5102-86f5-09f04cfa659e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410179} {:answer/id #uuid "8b0dcfdc-b7d8-5406-814d-16ab7d147b59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186410181}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410179} :answer-field/id #uuid "62b7e0f0-3a2a-5bad-a1a2-7313ccefaabb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410192}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=7{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2}+5{x}_{3}^{2}-4{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. "The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-10{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-4.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The  maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -5 \\ -5 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198444 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198090 :question/id #uuid "a6abb2f6-6e59-59ac-8549-62d25b3b6e9b" :question/math-academy-id "e-12664"} :knowledge-point/id $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-18{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+81{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that ${x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=9.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$ 

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -9 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -27 \\ -9 & 81\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -27 \\ -27 & 81\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & -27 \\ -27 & 81-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(81-\lambda )-729 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-90\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -90) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =0,\,90\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}=90.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186284645 :question/id #uuid "315ff370-acb2-54c0-a94c-7932c53e50d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-170525"} {:db/id 17592186284646 :question/id #uuid $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 8 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 16 \\ 8 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-20I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 16 \\ 16 & 4\end{aligned}]-20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 16 \\ 16 & -16\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

$$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q(x)‖ & =‖x‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{(\sqrt{6})}^{2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=18-18=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{9}^{2}+{6}^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186198750 :question/id #uuid "e6d806a7-8383-51f7-a460-be3b003d424b" :question/math-academy-id "q-177315"} {:db/id 17592186284748 :question/id #uuid "1e67e934-1049-5a47-aaca-94c1d2a3bfc1" :question/math-academy-id "q-177118" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "19a57218-72df-52b7-a7c9-b44507555a2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186281924} {:answer/id #uuid "236f86aa-fa00-5096-a10a-e7651f6a6f6c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186282002} {:answer/id #uuid "44f8d700-4e7f-5f15-911f-34b6d469a632" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186282274} {:answer/id #uuid "6d2190ba-be25-51f1-8832-021adf3dcc68" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186282623} {:answer/id #uuid "8f930388-ab9f-54e0-8499-291a03111580" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "None of the statements are true." :db/id 17592186282934}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186282934} :answer-field/id #uuid "4d6f2115-fb0f-5808-a58b-b7b09276ab3b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186284062}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

- Statement I is false since

$$

$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{2})$ since

Which of the following are orthogonal sets?

- $U={Q([\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}])}$
- $W={Q([\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}6 \\ -1\end{aligned}])}$
- $V={Q([\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]),Q([\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}])}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

Let's denote the elements of $U,W,$ and $V$ respectively as 

$\,$ ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})},\,$ ${Q({w}_{1}),Q({w}_{2})},\,$ and $\,{Q({v}_{1}),Q({v}_{2}),Q({v}_{3})}.$ 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthogonal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2})=0.$

- $Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2})=0,\,Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0,\,Q({v}_{2})\cdot Q({v}_{3})=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2}) & ={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=18-18=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthogonal.

- For the set $W,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({w}_{1})\cdot Q({w}_{2}) & ={w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=1-1=0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthogonal.

- For the Set $V,$ notice that 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q({v}_{1})\cdot Q({v}_{2}) & ={v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=2+12-5=9\ne 0.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$U$ and $W$ only"."} {:db/id 17592186411865 :question/id #uuid "8d807e12-6960-57f6-b74d-aa3fe66f0f76" :question/math-academy-id "q-178271" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198449 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4a5d6b1-e76a-5b33-8973-04d1d9062dc6" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Orthogonality of a Two-Vector Set"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "26beaa3c-ed64-5711-ae43-5915ddfb5a17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186411700} {:answer/id #uuid "3400f53e-dd72-52d4-80f7-e75f042482c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/id 17592186411703} {:answer/id #uuid "56148229-ce9a-5da3-a832-6f2fba7b9721" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements are true." :db/id 17592186411723} {:answer/id #uuid "7d45cde3-2e6d-51fc-a005-c567ebefb006" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186411744} {:answer/id #uuid "b96f5746-2e70-560e-b999-9a3896073130" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186411775}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "56148229-ce9a-5da3-a832-6f2fba7b9721" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements are true." :db/id 17592186411723} :answer-field/id #uuid "aafa25da-d701-5b8d-940d-a4b926749cbe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186411840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider a function $b(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{b(t)}=B(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{t}b(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{t}b(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{t}b(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{t}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-1)t}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $B(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-1)t}\,b(t)\,\text{d}t=B(s-1),
$$

where 

$$
s-1>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+1.

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=x+y,\,y(0)=0
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with two steps to approximate $y(1)$ and $y(2),$ rounded to two decimal places.

$$
y(1)≈{{field-1}},\,y(2)≈{{field-2}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

First, note that we are given $y(0)$ and asked to find $y(2).$ The distance from $x=0$ to $x=2$ is $2,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-0}{2}=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((x+y)+({x}_{\text{new}}+{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y)+\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve for the general formula for ${y}_{\text{new}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{y}_{\text{new}} & =\frac{1}{2}(x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y) \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to calculate our approximations of $y(1)$ and $y(2).$

**Step 1**.

From the initial conditions, we have

$$
x=0,\,y=0.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=0+1=1.
$$

$$

From the previous step, we have

$$
x=1,\,y=1.
$$

Therefore, the new $x$ value is 

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Hence, the new $y$ value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =x+{x}_{\text{new}}+3y \\  & =1+2+3\cdot 1 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{At})=A\,{e}^{At}.

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=2x-2y-3,\,y(0)=1
$$

To approximate the solution, one step of the Runge-Kutta method has already been computed, resulting in the following estimate:

$$
y(1)≈0
$$

Use the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method with one step to approximate $y(2).$

*Hint: The corrector equation of the two-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is defined as*

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx
$$

*where ${y}_{p}$ denotes the predictor at the current step, and ${y}_{-1}^{′}$ is the estimated slope at the previous point.*" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the $2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM $2$-step) Method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- ${y}^{′}=f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- ${y}_{-1}^{′}=f({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point (${x}_{-1},{y}_{-1}),$ and

- ${y}_{p}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{p})=(x+Δx,y+Δ{y}_{p}).$

Before we start, let's add the initial condition data and Runge-Kutta step data to a table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Now, since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

First, we compute the values of ${y}^{′}$ at each point according to the given rule:

- The slope at the previous point $({x}_{-1},{y}_{-1})=(0,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{-1}^{′} & =2{x}_{-1}-2{y}_{-1}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 0-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

- The slope at the current point $(x,y)=(1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2x-2y-3 \\  & =2\cdot 1-2\cdot 0-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ |  |  |  |  |

Next, we compute $Δ{y}_{p}$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

So, the coordinates of the predicted new point are

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+1=2, \\ {y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p}=0+1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's add the second value to the table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ |  |  |

Hence, the slope at this predicted point is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =2{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p}-3 \\  & =2\cdot 2-2\cdot 1-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ |  |

Finally, we compute $Δy$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{′}+8{y}^{′}-{y}_{-1}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot (-1)+8\cdot (-1)-(-5))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot (-8) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |

The value of $x$ in the next row is ${x}_{\text{new}}=2.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $Δy$ to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\  & =0+(-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,{y}^{′}\,$ | $Δ{y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}$ | ${y}_{p}^{′}$ | $Δy$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-5$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{2}{3}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

17592186308207}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y=0,\,y(1)=-1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2
$$

Use Euler's Method with two steps to approximate $y(2)$ and ${y}^{′}(2).$

$$
y(2)≈{{field-1}},\,{y}^{′}(2)≈{{field-2}}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a second-order initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=f(x,y,{y}^{′}),\,y(a)=c,\,{y}^{′}(a)=d,
$$

we can use Euler's method to approximate a solution by first reducing the second-order ODE to a system of first-order ODEs,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(a)=c, \\ {z}^{′}=f(x,y,z)\, & z(a)=d,\end{aligned}
$$

before applying the update rule component-wise to each equation.

To apply Euler’s method, we first isolate ${y}^{″}$ so it can serve as the derivative of a new variable $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+4{y}^{′}-y & =0 \\ {x}^{2}{y}^{″} & =y-4{y}^{′} \\ {y}^{″} & =\frac{y-4{y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute our new variable $z={y}^{′},{z}^{′}={y}^{″}$ in the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Note that the initial value of $z$ is $z(1)={y}^{′}(1)=2.$
So, the initial value problem reduces to the following system of first-order ODEs:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=z,\, & y(1)=-1, \\ {z}^{′}=\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}},\, & z(1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can proceed with Euler's method by applying the update rule component-wise.

First, note that we are given the values of $y$ and $z={y}^{′}$ at $x=1$ and asked to find their values at $x=2.$ The distance from $x=1$ to $x=2$ is $1,$ and since we are asked to use two steps of equal size, our step size must be

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we'll start by creating a table that includes the initial condition data $y(1)=-1$ and $z(1)=2.$

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ |  |  | $2$ |  |  |

**Step 1**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the first row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=2 \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{-1-4\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}}=-9 \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=2\cdot \frac{1}{2}=1 \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=-9\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{9}{2} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=1+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=-1+1=0 \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=2-\frac{9}{2}=-\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{2}$ |  |  |

**Step 2**.

We compute ${y}^{′}$ and $Δy,$ ${z}^{′}$ and $Δz$ (using the values of $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ in the second row), and the values of ${x}_{\text{new}},$ ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and ${z}_{\text{new}}$ using Euler's method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =z=-\frac{5}{2} \\ {z}^{′} & =\frac{y-4z}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{0-4(-\frac{5}{2})}{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{10}{(\frac{9}{4})}=\frac{40}{9} \\ Δy & ={y}^{′}\cdot Δx=-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ Δz & ={z}^{′}\cdot Δx=\frac{40}{9}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=\frac{20}{9} \\ {x}_{\text{new}} & =x+Δx=\frac{3}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=2 \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy=0-\frac{5}{4}=-\frac{5}{4} \\ {z}_{\text{new}} & =z+Δz=-\frac{5}{2}+\frac{20}{9}=-\frac{5}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

We add these values to our table.

| $x$ | $y$ | ${y}^{′}$ | $Δy$ | $z$ | ${z}^{′}$ | $Δz$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $2$ | $-9$ | $-\frac{9}{2}$ |
| $\frac{3}{2}$ | $0$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ | $\frac{40}{9}$ | $\frac{20}{9}$ |
| $2$ | $-\frac{5}{4}$ |  |  | $-\frac{5}{18}$ |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that
$y(2)≈-\frac{5}{4}$

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For which of the following values is the implicit Euler method stable, given that $\lambda $ is the parameter of the test equation?

I. $\lambda Δx=0.1$

II. $\lambda Δx=0.8$

III. $\lambda Δx=1.2$

IV. $\lambda Δx=5$

*Hint: The stability function $R$ of the implicit Euler method is given by*

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=\frac{1}{1+\lambda Δx}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method 
${y}_{n+1}={y}_{n}+Δ{y}_{n}$
is stable for a given step size $Δx$ if, when applied to the test equation

$$
{y}^{′}=-\lambda y,\,y(0)=1,\,x\ge 0,\,\lambda >0,
$$

the numerical solution satisfies ${y}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty ,$ just like the exact solution.

When a method is applied to the test equation, the update takes the form

$$
{y}_{n+1}=R(\lambda Δx){y}_{n},
$$

where $R(\lambda Δx)$ is referred to as the stability function of the method. The set of values for which the method is stable, given by $|R(\lambda Δx)|<1,$ is called the stability region of the method.

The stability function of the implicit Euler method is

$$
R(\lambda Δx)=\frac{1}{1+\lambda Δx}.
$$

Let's check the stability of the implicit Euler Method for each of the given values in turn.

- For $\lambda Δx=0.1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.1)| & =|\frac{1}{1+0.1}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{1.1}| \\  & =0.9090…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=0.8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(0.8)| & =|\frac{1}{1+0.8}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{1.8}| \\  & =0.5555…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=1.2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(1.2)| & =|\frac{1}{1+1.2}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{2.2}| \\  & =0.4545…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

- For $\lambda Δx=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|R(5)| & =|\frac{1}{1+5}| \\  & =|\frac{1}{6}| \\  & =0.1666…<1.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since this value falls *within* the stability region, the implicit Euler method is stable.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, III, and IV".

Note that, since the implicit Euler method is absolutely stable, it is stable for all possible values of $\lambda Δx.$"} {:db/id 17592186229156 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}-y,\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example  $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({x}^{2}-y)+({x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}),\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}})=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}).
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2}-1+{2}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}(0+4-{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}-3.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308572 :question/id #uuid "5954fe07-ca71-56cd-b722-9e93582b85a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-334151"} {:db/id 17592186377165 :question/id #uuid "b37ab3c3-9716-5054-bac9-1caa7318af92" :question/math-academy-id "q-334079"} {:db/id 17592186391387 :question/id #uuid "c3e7b77a-8724-5c98-839a-9b13b32a04b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-334077" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a65f23d9-ece1-5d94-9f1b-4fa3ff21de35" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186391389} {:answer/id #uuid "cb9d2a40-8db7-58a2-965b-5f8b9284015a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-2\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-1" :db/id 17592186391390} {:answer/id #uuid "04c655f7-87ce-528a-8800-3f6394ecdb07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-1" :db/id 17592186391391} {:answer/id #uuid "f96ae150-da92-5738-ba1d-d4d1763de606" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-2\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186391392} {:answer/id #uuid "838f71c2-360e-538a-95d7-8b3b5dc7a597" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-2\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-2" :db/id 17592186391393}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186391392} :answer-field/id #uuid "df1f67de-316f-5c29-b742-1caa63eae0d6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186391388}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$

$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?" :question/worked-solution "For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}})\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-1-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}\sqrt{1} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-2\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186229157 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186228908 :question/id #uuid "d77c4a1b-863b-57ad-be77-44f2d802f554" :question/math-academy-id "e-21677"} :knowledge-point/id
