17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c6e87982-ab6f-5e96-94e7-996ae7f3b605" :question/math-academy-id "q-338845" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-10\lambda {y}^{′}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda  & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}5\lambda  & 1+5\lambda  \\ 1+10\lambda  & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "10ec5288-96c7-54f4-a406-4dc3fa372454" :question/math-academy-id "q-338917" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+9\lambda y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(3)=0,\,0\le x\le 3,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(3)=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+9\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 3\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })+3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(3)=0$ yields

$$
-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(9\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
9\sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{81}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "35485800-4576-505b-b01c-a3a46dd2634c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418252}} {:db/id 17592186418252 :step/content {:db/id 17592186391720 :question/answer-fields {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2b03c659-cc6c-5259-9cfb-c53b896cc809" :question/math-academy-id "q-338909" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter value corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda \pi )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
4\lambda \pi =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{4}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bab35c78-7682-5ede-95d9-455d7d62484b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418251}} {:db/id 17592186418254 :step/content {:db/id 17592186314744 :question/answer-fields boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda  & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda  & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1).
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$"} :step/id #uuid "db32b2ae-bde3-5b8b-9a23-8d2e69b2eb90" Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda  & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}5\lambda  & 1+5\lambda  \\ 1+10\lambda  & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$"} :step/id #uuid "10ec5288-96c7-54f4-a406-4dc3fa372454" 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b2709e91-93e6-520b-8d50-587e1e5c8629" :question/math-academy-id "q-338904" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda  & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda  & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1).
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$"} :step/id #uuid "db32b2ae-bde3-5b8b-9a23-8d2e69b2eb90" :question/math-academy-id "q-338917" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+9\lambda y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(3)=0,\,0\le x\le 3,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(3)=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+9\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 3\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda })+3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+3B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(3)=0$ yields

$$
-3A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(9\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
9\sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{81}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "35485800-4576-505b-b01c-a3a46dd2634c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418252}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "333487d5-2b4f-53f7-a1f4-c935ce9920e2" :answer/type {:db/id $$

Applying the boundary condition $y(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi \sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
4\pi \sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}}{16}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.

:question/math-academy-id "q-338909" :question/problem "Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$" :question/worked-solution "We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter value corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda x)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+4B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-4A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\lambda \pi )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
4\lambda \pi =n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{n}{4}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bab35c78-7682-5ede-95d9-455d7d62484b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418251}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80717e13-aa04-534e-b7cb-b9dd198b1171" :answer/type {:db/id [{:db/id 17592186162849 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163224 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $A$ is an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix over $\mathbb{R}.$ The **spectral theorem** states the following:

- The eigenvalues of $A$ are all real.
- The eigenvectors corresponding to *different* eigenvalues are orthogonal.
- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
- $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable." :tutorial/id #uuid "5ecbbdd0-25a0-52ee-8f0c-987dcd8ba584" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4882 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "84b2f14e-f6c7-5b6c-b6d7-19d4d7d71f71" :step/math-academy-id 30533 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162902}} {:db/id 17592186162902 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162013 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161805 :question/id #uuid "6ae71f41-133f-50b6-a286-20ae7e2c3a9d" :question/math-academy-id "e-8291"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c67d532-acd9-5231-a27f-d39084863e01" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048493}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162645} {:db/id 17592186162659} {:db/id 17592186365052} {:db/id 17592186366636} {:db/id 17592186366643} {:db/id 17592186366650} {:db/id 17592186366657} {:db/id 17592186411856}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements Regarding the Spectral Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "95f72e96-f84b-5b21-a070-253638be57a8" :step/math-academy-id 30970 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162903}} {:db/id 17592186162903 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163243 :tutorial/content "We can write an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix $A$ in terms of a sum of products of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Specifically, if $\mathbf{u}_i$ denotes an orthonormal eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$, then

$$A=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T.$$

Expressing a symmetric matrix $A$ in this way is called the **spectral decomposition** of $A.$

To demonstrate, let's find the spectral decomposition of the $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ given by

$$A = [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].$$

The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1 = 6$ and $\lambda_2 = -4,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are

$$\mathbf{v}_1 = [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \quad \textrm{and} \quad \mathbf{v}_2 = [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$$

The spectral decomposition of $A$ is given by

$$A =\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1 \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2 \mathbf u_2^T,$$

**spectral theorem** states the following:

Specifically, if $\mathbf{u}_i$ denotes an orthonormal eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ for $i=1,\ldots, n$, then

$$A=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T.$$

Expressing a symmetric matrix $A$ in this way is called the **spectral decomposition** of $A.$

To demonstrate, let's find the spectral decomposition of the $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ given by

$$A = [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].$$

The eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1 = 6$ and $\lambda_2 = -4,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are

$$\mathbf{v}_1 = [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \quad \textrm{and} \quad \mathbf{v}_2 = [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$$

The spectral decomposition of $A$ is given by

$$A =\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1 \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2 \mathbf u_2^T,$$

where $\mathbf u_1$ and $\mathbf u_2$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2,$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}$$

Therefore, the spectral decomposition of $A$ is

$$\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\ & =6\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\ & =6\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3\end{aligned}]+(-4)\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\ & ={{6}_{⏟}}_{{\lambda }_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} & \frac{3}{10} \\ \frac{3}{10} & \frac{9}{10}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}}+{{(-4)}_{⏟}}_{{\lambda }_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & -\frac{3}{10} \\ -\frac{3}{10} & \frac{1}{10}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T}}.\end{aligned}$$

In this decomposition, the matrix $\mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T$ is the orthogonal projection matrix that maps any $\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2$ onto the subspace spanned by $\mathbf u_i.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a90957e3-e4b9-548d-930b-e060c6b63859" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4973 :tutorial/title "The Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "8df507ec-4d53-59f1-b941-07907cd14b6f" :step/math-academy-id 30971 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162905}} {:db/id 17592186163243 :tutorial/content "We can write an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix $A$ in terms of a sum of products of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "69f0b9bd-9336-5c1c-91e3-bf72b33b1333" :question/math-academy-id "q-140847" :question/problem "Suppose that

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$

are eigenvectors of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ respectively. Find the matrix $A.$" :question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {u}_{2} & =\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}{u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}{u}_{2}^{T} \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]+8\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "07386288-c5f3-55df-b73a-99cec25cb7d6"} {:db/id 17592186407555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162646 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1556dc1b-0c8b-54e0-a340-18371f592ed3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407520} {:answer/id #uuid "286d06a8-1050-59ed-a665-558d840c2aae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407525} {:answer/id #uuid "d6effcc8-e643-5b20-9090-b3855faacab9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407541} {:answer/id #uuid "e9f4f75f-447a-5e0c-a1d6-feae985a30a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407543} {:answer/id #uuid "f93a6cf9-78b6-546d-ba88-361fc48a056a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407544}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407544} :answer-field/id #uuid "ebade115-5b0c-52d7-94cc-8ec9e5babad9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407549}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "11bdef24-ff68-513b-bfa6-5f2fb8c78b02" :question/math-academy-id "q-94768" :question/problem "Find the orthogonal projection matrix that maps $x\in {R}^{2}$ onto the subspace spanned by an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-4$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =-4.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$\lambda =2$ of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "The spectral decomposition of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A={\lambda }_{1}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}^{T}+{\lambda }_{2}{u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}^{T},
$$

where ${u}_{1}$ and ${u}_{2}$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively.

Moreover, ${u}_{i}\cdot {u}_{i}^{T}$ is the projection matrix corresponding to ${u}_{i}.$

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda =2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 18\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -4 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 16 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖v‖=\sqrt{17}.$ Dividing $v$ by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector: 

$$
u=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot {u}^{T} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{17}}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{17}[\begin{aligned}16 & 4 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "61132d09-e84e-51b9-b83a-aedca27c1563" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407558}} {:db/id 17592186407556 :step/content {:db/id 17592186407551 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16877fa0-d3a3-5da8-ba77-c7e71244a7c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407521} {:answer/id #uuid "6d264661-257d-5c8a-8684-122b5c0a6807" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407531} {:answer/id #uuid "9555f6b0-dd96-561e-b956-a28b10613e7e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-8 & 6 \\ 6 & -3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407535} {:answer/id #uuid "ad0b779d-af50-58f8-97aa-dd75027108dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}5 & -6 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407536} {:answer/id #uuid "d6231cbd-de79-555a-b056-b8008595ed25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-5 & 6 \\ 6 & -3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186407540}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407531} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1092e23-b9a3-5556-b0d1-0745f95be4b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407548}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7e3f233e-913d-50cf-8912-1c6832afca12" :question/math-academy-id "q-95725" :question/problem "Suppose that

2128} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134689 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135056 :tutorial/content "Consider the subspace $V=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3\},$ where

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

We already know how to find an orthogonal basis for $2$-dimensional subspaces. But, how can we do it for subspaces with higher dimensions, like $V?$

Good news is that we can extend the **Gram-Schmidt process**. Since the first two vectors are already orthogonal, we proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows:

**Step 1**: We set $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

**Step 2**: We set $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$

**Step 3**. Next, let $S=\textrm{Span}(\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2).$ We find ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3}$ using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{S}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\  & ={a}_{3}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}-\frac{{a}_{3}\cdot {v}_{2}}{{v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}}{v}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/5b/5b52c26738f2b4dd577ab4148ef7673ad4a1aa53c82a6a6c1e7bf46c0ff36df0.png)

Notice that $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3$ is written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}),$ $\mathbf{a}_2(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}),$ and $\mathbf{a}_3.$ This means that ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3} \in V,$ and also ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3} \perp S.$ Moreover, 

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3} \}.
$$

 

Applying the formula for $\mathbf{v}_3$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{3} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-(\frac{2}{2})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-(-\frac{3}{3})[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "066a02aa-4c3e-5e75-8147-7e723bac3b9e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3633 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9b8d3614-1e0d-5f26-94a2-81b1f24e5df1" :step/math-academy-id 20262 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134690}} {:db/id 17592186134690 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133796 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133605 :question/id #uuid "683556db-c65d-5279-ac14-7dfaa496db0a" :question/math-academy-id "e-5584"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f585bd05-7dac-55b1-a0ab-f8320242a5df" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050578}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134314} {:db/id 17592186134360} {:db/id 17592186326922} {:db/id 17592186360629} {:db/id 17592186360630}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Orthogonal Basis of a Span Given Some Orthogonal Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "9ca65108-e04c-5dd4-9c81-fa10af333e97" :step/math-academy-id 20263 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134797}} {:db/id 17592186134691 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135057 :tutorial/content "But what do we do if the original basis we are given doesn't contain any orthogonal vectors? Well, then we make them orthogonal using the Gram-Schmidt process!

Given a basis $\,\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{a}_n\}$ for a non zero subspace $V$, we can get an orthogonal basis for $V$ by defining the vectors

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & ={a}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\ {v}_{3} & ={a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{3}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{3} \\ ⋮\,\, & =\,⋮ \\ {v}_{n} & ={a}_{n}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{n}-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{2}}\,{a}_{n}-⋯-{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{n-1}}\,{a}_{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

The set of vectors $\{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2,\ldots, \mathbf{v}_n\}$ will be an orthogonal basis for $V$.

Here, we build up the orthogonal basis one vector at a time, by taking away from each basis vector its orthogonal projection onto each of the $1$-dimensional subspaces spanned by one of the orthogonal basis vectors found already.

Furthermore, if we want to find an *orthonormal* basis, we just have to normalize the vectors $\mathbf{v}_i$ for $i=1,2,\dots,n.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a3f649a6-0268-539c-a952-a33eeaa25744" $$\mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\quad A \quad} \mathbb{R}^m,$$

there are **four fundamental subspaces** that naturally occur. The first two are as follows:

- The **column space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ This is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $A.$
- The **null space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ This is the set of all vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that, when pre-multiplied by $A,$ result in the zero-vector $\mathbf{0}.$

Now, notice that the transpose $A^T$ is an $n \times m$ matrix and can be considered as the transformation

$$\mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\quad A^T \quad} \mathbb{R}^n.$$

So, we have similar subspaces for the transpose $A^T{:}$

- The column space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ We call this the **row space** of $A$ since the span of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to the span of the rows of $A.$
- The null space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ We call this the **left null space** of $A$ since it is equivalent to the set of all vectors $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m$ such that $\mathbf y^T A = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's discuss how these spaces relate to each other:

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are orthogonal complements of each other: $$\text{Col}(A^T) = \text{Null}(A)^\perp$$
- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ that are orthogonal complements of each other: $$\text{Col}(A) = \text{Null}(A^T)^\perp$$

The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/ce/ced4191955b6886491bf612c62344d2faf6e7fe8d49884446de0eb86851d22e8.png)

To see why $\text{Col}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Null}(A^T),$ note the following:

- When calculating the product $A^T \mathbf x,$ we multiply each row of $A^T$ by $\mathbf x.$
- Suppose that $\mathbf x\in \text{Null}(A^T).$ Then, by definition, $A^T \mathbf x = \mathbf 0.$
- Thus, $\mathbf x$ must be orthogonal to each row of $A^T.$ Equivalently, this means that $\mathbf x$ is orthogonal to each *column* of $A.$
- Hence, $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A).$

We can deduce that $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ by similar reasoning." :tutorial/id #uuid "2b6f45b1-7cfa-5c62-9928-caeff36d1cc0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5443 "f70134b1-0b93-5597-a6b6-16fdc7fb1bad" :step/math-academy-id 33937 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134840}} {:db/id 17592186134839 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135111 :tutorial/content "Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A,$ what is the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under $A?$

Note that pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ by $A$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A{:}$ $$\underbrace{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} & ⋯ & {a}_{n} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{\large A} \cdot \underbrace{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{\large \mathbf{x}} = x_1 [\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{1} \\ |\end{aligned}] + x_2 [\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{2} \\ |\end{aligned}] +\cdots+ x_n [\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{n} \\ |\end{aligned}]$$

Therefore, by definition, the image of $\mathbb{R}^n$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ the column space of $A.$

![](images/db/dbefb436195af5ffa8841f4119054426db50ac2987138a5912991cf42321e0dc.png)

Similarly, pre-multiplying a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ by $A^T$ gives a linear combination of the columns of $A^T{:}$ $$\underbrace{[\begin{aligned}| & | & ⋯ & | \\ {a}_{1}^{T} & {a}_{2}^{T} & ⋯ & {a}_{m}^{T} \\ | & | & ⋯ & |\end{aligned}]}_{\large A^T} \cdot \underbrace{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{m}\end{aligned}]}_{\large \mathbf{x}} = x_1 [\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{1}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}] + x_2 [\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{2}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}] +\cdots+ x_m [\begin{aligned}| \\ {a}_{m}^{T} \\ |\end{aligned}]$$

Therefore, the image of $\mathbb{R}^m$ under the action of $A^T$ must be $\text{Col}(A^T).$ This is also the row space of $A,$ since a linear combination of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to a linear combination of the rows of $A.$

![](images/c8/c82ab88289fc2d35ce354933937d908c54a9839bfa0fd126187a9723c58eeb27.png)

We can use similar reasoning to find the image of the four fundamental subspaces under the appropriate matrix." :tutorial/id #uuid "915420e9-f241-5e99-8274-32ffdfb79b9a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5454 :tutorial/title "Images Under the Action of a Matrix and Its Transpose"} :step/id #uuid "e8b74e81-7593-5f0a-9136-22383330a688" :step/math-academy-id 33950 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134838}} {:db/id 17592186134840 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135112 :tutorial/content "Consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with rank $r.$ The dimensions of the four fundamental subspaces of $A$ are as follows:

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.$ Since the column space is the span of the columns of $A,$ its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is $\text{rank}(A)=r.$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that $$\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.$$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that $$\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

![](images/1c/1c550b87048bba6a7c362f00f09faca74ca9b056a93698436d0994c120971356.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "40af35b2-abb6-59b8-999a-9976edbb9ce8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5455 :tutorial/title "Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} :step/id #uuid "957cde37-32d4-515e-ad96-75c96f7bfa57" :step/math-academy-id 33951 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134837}} {:db/id 17592186134841 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135113 :tutorial/content "Let's review what we have learned in this lesson.

If we consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$ as a transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m,$ then there are four fundamental subspaces of $A{:}$

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with dimensions $r$ and $m-r,$ respectively.
- $\text{Col}(A^T)$ and $\text{Null}(A)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with dimensions $r$ and $n-r,$ respectively.

Furthermore,

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ and
- $\text{Null}(A)$ and $\text{Col}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^n.$

Finally, we have that

- the image of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ and
- the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of $A^T$ is $\text{Col}(A^T).$

These facts about the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/37/37f633d0bca1a599f7d1658c051f802da5d607d420beeb4bddbef5cd98c366ef.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "190e1777-4f27-5c94-88bd-21c9992eb024" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5456 :tutorial/title "The Big Picture of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} :step/id #uuid "8eef352e-273a-5614-b97d-8c357807e9a0" :step/math-academy-id 33952}] :activity/title "The Four Fundamental Subspaces of a Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134041} {:db/id 17592186134834 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135110 :tutorial/content "When considering an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ as a linear transformation

$$\mathbb{R}^n \xrightarrow{\quad A \quad} \mathbb{R}^m,$$

there are **four fundamental subspaces** that naturally occur. The first two are as follows:

- The **column space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ This is the set of all linear combinations of the columns of $A.$
- The **null space** of $A,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ This is the set of all vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that, when pre-multiplied by $A,$ result in the zero-vector $\mathbf{0}.$

Now, notice that the transpose $A^T$ is an $n \times m$ matrix and can be considered as the transformation

$$\mathbb{R}^m \xrightarrow{\quad A^T \quad} \mathbb{R}^n.$$

So, we have similar subspaces for the transpose $A^T{:}$

- The column space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Col}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n.$ We call this the **row space** of $A$ since the span of the columns of $A^T$ is equivalent to the span of the rows of $A.$
- The null space of $A^T,$ denoted $\text{Null}(A^T),$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m.$ We call this the **left null space** of $A$ since it is equivalent to the set of all vectors $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m$ such that $\mathbf y^T A = \mathbf{0}.$

Let's discuss how these spaces relate to each other:

- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that are orthogonal complements of each other: $$\text{Col}(A^T) = \text{Null}(A)^\perp$$
- We have two subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ that are orthogonal complements of each other: $$\text{Col}(A) = \text{Null}(A^T)^\perp$$

The four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

![](images/ce/ced4191955b6886491bf612c62344d2faf6e7fe8d49884446de0eb86851d22e8.png)

To see why $\text{Col}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Null}(A^T),$ note the following:

- When calculating the product $A^T \mathbf x,$ we multiply each row of $A^T$ by $\mathbf x.$
- Suppose that $\mathbf x\in \text{Null}(A^T).$ Then, by definition, $A^T \mathbf x = \mathbf 0.$
- Thus, $\mathbf x$ must be orthogonal to each row of $A^T.$ Equivalently, this means that $\mathbf x$ is orthogonal to each *column* of $A.$
- Hence, $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is orthogonal to $\text{Col}(A).$

We can deduce that $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ by similar reasoning." :tutorial/id #uuid "2b6f45b1-7cfa-5c62-9928-caeff36d1cc0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5443 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f59f0795-5e5a-517e-8142-7251b3810d58" :step/math-academy-id 33903 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134835}} {:db/id 17592186135110 :tutorial/content "When considering an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ as a linear transformation

- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A)) = r.$ Since the column space is the span of the columns of $A,$ its dimension is the number of linearly independent columns which, by Gaussian elimination, is $\text{rank}(A)=r.$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T)) = r.$ It can be shown that the dimension of the row space of $A$ also equals $r.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(A^T)=\text{rank}(A)=r.$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = n-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ we have that $$\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)}_{n} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A^T))}_{r} = n-r.$$
- $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = m-r.$ Since $\text{Null}(A^T)$ is the orthogonal complement of $\text{Col}(A)$ in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ we have that $$\text{dim}(\text{Null}(A^T)) = \underbrace{\text{dim}(\mathbb{R}^m)}_{m} - \underbrace{\text{dim}(\text{Col}(A))}_{r} = m-r.$$

Let's add these dimensions to the diagram below.

![](images/1c/1c550b87048bba6a7c362f00f09faca74ca9b056a93698436d0994c120971356.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "40af35b2-abb6-59b8-999a-9976edbb9ce8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5455 :tutorial/title "Dimensions of the Four Fundamental Subspaces"} {:db/id 17592186135113 :tutorial/content "Let's review what we have learned in this lesson.

If we consider an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$ as a transformation from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to $\mathbb{R}^m,$ then there are four fundamental subspaces of $A{:}$

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with dimensions $r$ and $m-r,$ respectively.
- $\text{Col}(A^T)$ and $\text{Null}(A)$ are subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with dimensions $r$ and $n-r,$ respectively.

Furthermore,

- $\text{Col}(A)$ and $\text{Null}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^m,$ and
- $\text{Null}(A)$ and $\text{Col}(A^T)$ are orthogonal complements in $\mathbb{R}^n.$

Finally, we have that

- the image of $\text{Col}(A^T)$ under the action of $A$ is $\text{Col}(A),$ and
- the image of $\text{Col}(A)$ under the action of $A^T$ is $\text{Col}(A^T).$

These facts about the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix $A$ can be schematically visualized, as shown below.

{:db/id 17592186167791 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168149 :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

> *Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*
> 
> 
> $$
> f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
> $$

For example, let's find the average value of the function 

\[
f(x,y) =x+3y^2+2
\]

over the region 

\[
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
\] 

Earlier, we found that 

\[
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = 28, \qquad \textrm{Area}(D) = 4.
\]

Therefore, the average value of the function over [math]D[/math] is

\begin{align*}
f_{\textrm{ave}}  	

&= \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt]

&= \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 28 \\[5pt]

&=  7. 
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

> *If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*
> 
> 
> $$
> \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
> $$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. $$
f(x,y) = x+3y^2+2
$$

and the region $D$ given by

$$
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
$$

According to the mean value theorem for double integrals, there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that

$$
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
$$

Evaluating the integral on the left-hand side, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+3{y}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[xy+{y}^{3}+2y]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2x+12)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{2}+12x]}_{x=0}^{x=2} \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4.
$$

So, our mean-value equation simplifies to

$$
\begin{aligned}28 & =f(a,b)\cdot 4 \\ 7 & =f(a,b) \\ 7 & =a+3{b}^{2}+2 \\ a & =5-3{b}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation describes part of a parabola in the $xy$-plane, as shown below.

![](images/46/46873c4ecb290380488e589082fc0759324d3540494f5b83e2d64db5d9cdf62a.png)

To find a particular point that satisfies the mean value theorem, we can set, for example, $b=1 \in [0,2]$ and obtain $a=2.$ So, the point $(2,1)$ satisfies the mean value theorem for double integrals. Consequently, the two solids below must have the same volume.

![](images/82/82d3a762ab323339570e6010038e75ce95f3fdbde958a2ffa876972cbf91e8fb.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "b890c915-3364-5ac3-b88b-298ed92d9def" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7784 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "32b5b570-9467-5bff-bc3b-29964ed86c09" :step/math-academy-id 45050 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167790}}] :activity/title "The Average Value of a Multivariable Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166974} {:db/id 17592186167794 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168150 :tutorial/content "Given a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $[a, b],$ the mean value theorem for integrals guarantees that there exists a number $c \in [a,b]$ such that

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a),
$$

which can be visualized as shown below.

![](images/0a/0afb9b15787eb89f73f322290bdbe2288027c54924d274c438773ce151a17291.png)

We have a similar theorem for functions with two variables. The so-called **mean value theorem for double integrals** states:

> *If the function $f(x,y)$ is continuous on a closed and bounded region $D,$ then there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that*
> 
> 
> $$
> \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = f(a,b) \cdot \textrm{Area}(D).
> $$

This has a nice geometrical interpretation when $f$ is non-negative on $D.$ In this case, the theorem tells us that there exists a point $(a,b) \in D$ such that the volume of the solid enclosed between the surface $z=f(x,y)$ and the $xy$-plane over the region $D$ equals the volume of the right cylinder with base $D$ and height $f(a,b).$ 

The diagram below shows the case when $D$ is rectangular, and the corresponding cylinder is a rectangular solid.

![](images/8e/8ed477207ee61fbdaf963ed8a127e3f1d4cf76707d2eeb4b450fd49f78e15b7e.png)

In general, the point $(a,b)$ mentioned in the theorem is not unique. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "b65eeb5f-8a44-55b9-819c-1c6c0d979d1e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7778 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "037c5a22-eee3-557c-b683-370d2389ad82" :step/math-academy-id 45031 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167795}} {:db/id 17592186167790 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166883 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166488 :question/id #uuid "22a44ff4-55e7-51db-a54e-26ef23764fa4" :question/math-academy-id "e-12490"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d13b0d31-65b8-550f-b97b-f4ece63bf834" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049280} {:db/id 17592186049997} {:db/id 17592186050264}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167132} {:db/id 17592186167133} {:db/id 17592186281612} {:db/id 17592186281614} {:db/id 17592186281634} {:db/id 17592186281635}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "360dd2dd-b48a-554c-9341-3a3e93d1e334" :step/math-academy-id 44978 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167791}} {:db/id 17592186167791 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168149 :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

$$
f_\textrm{ave} = \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Length}(D)}\int_a^b f(x) \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

There is an analogous definition for functions of two variables, stated below:

> *Suppose $D$ is a closed and bounded region in $\mathbb{R}^2$ which has non-zero finite area $\textrm{Area}(D).$ If $f (x, y)$ is a continuous function on $D,$ then **the average value of $\boldsymbol f$ on $\boldsymbol D$** is given by*
> 
> 
> $$
> f_{\textrm{ave}} =\dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A.
> $$

For example, let's find the average value of the function 

\[
f(x,y) =x+3y^2+2
\]

over the region 

\[
D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.
\] 

Earlier, we found that 

\[
\iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A = 28, \qquad \textrm{Area}(D) = 4.
\]

Therefore, the average value of the function over [math]D[/math] is

\begin{align*}
f_{\textrm{ave}}  	

&= \dfrac{1}{\textrm{Area}(D)} \, \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt]

&= \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot 28 \\[5pt]

&=  7. 
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "c862ff42-4e5b-5bbb-aed6-3d9760d339b1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7770 :tutorial/title "The Average Value of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "c77b7ad4-9d8d-58f4-bd79-4c0b0b47cfea" :step/math-academy-id 44981 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167792}} {:db/id 17592186168149 :tutorial/content "Recall that the average value of a continuous function $f(x)$ on a closed interval $D = [a,b]$ is given by

:step/content {:db/id 17592186135083 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{0}^{1}\int_{x}^{2x} (x-2y) \ \mathrm{d}  y \ \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

Notice that the domain of integration is a type I region. 

To compute this integral, we must bear the following important points in mind.

- We start with the inner integral, as usual.

- When integrating with respect to $y,$ we treat $x$ as though it were a constant.

- The limits of integration for the inner integral are functions of $x.$ Once again, we treat $x$ as though it were a constant and substitute the integration limits as usual. After this step, there should be no more $y$'s in our integral.

- Finally, we compute the outer integral.

Let's apply these steps to solve the given problem.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{2x}(x-2y)\text{ }dy]\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[xy-{y}^{2}]_{x}^{2x}\text{ }dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x\cdot (2x)-{(2x)}^{2}]-[x\cdot (x)-(x)^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[2{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}]-[{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx & =-2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{[{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}[{1}^{3}-{0}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}

17592186134756}} {:db/id 17592186134756 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135083 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to evaluate the repeated integral

$$
\int_{0}^{1}\int_{x}^{2x} (x-2y) \ \mathrm{d}  y \ \mathrm{d}  x.
$$

Notice that the domain of integration is a type I region. 

To compute this integral, we must bear the following important points in mind.

- We start with the inner integral, as usual.

- When integrating with respect to $y,$ we treat $x$ as though it were a constant.

- The limits of integration for the inner integral are functions of $x.$ Once again, we treat $x$ as though it were a constant and substitute the integration limits as usual. After this step, there should be no more $y$'s in our integral.

- Finally, we compute the outer integral.

Let's apply these steps to solve the given problem.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{2x}(x-2y)\text{ }dy]\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[xy-{y}^{2}]_{x}^{2x}\text{ }dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x\cdot (2x)-{(2x)}^{2}]-[x\cdot (x)-(x)^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[2{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}]-[{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx & =-2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{[{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}[{1}^{3}-{0}^{3}] \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3698e7e3-4bc2-5db0-96b5-172131284b4a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4262 :tutorial/title "Evaluating Repeated Integrals With Variable Limits"} :step/id #uuid "59bc86e8-4dae-564b-ab2b-c8ac5309d3be" :step/math-academy-id 25908 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134757}} {:db/id 17592186135083 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to evaluate the repeated integral

- Finally, we compute the outer integral.

Let's apply these steps to solve the given problem.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y,$ treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{x}^{2x}(x-2y)\text{ }dy]\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[xy-{y}^{2}]_{x}^{2x}\text{ }dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[x\cdot (2x)-{(2x)}^{2}]-[x\cdot (x)-(x)^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[2{x}^{2}-4{x}^{2}]-[{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}-2{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,dx\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "39356ac1-0a31-5e6e-9a6f-6a96bbbbe55c" :question/math-academy-id "q-37683" :question/problem "Calculate ${\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1/x}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx.$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1/x}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}[{\int }_{x}^{1/x}y\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{x}^{1/x}dx \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2})dx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}-1)\,dx & =\frac{1}{2}{[-\frac{1}{3{x}^{3}}-x]}_{1/2}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}[\frac{1}{3}+1-(\frac{8}{3}+\frac{1}{2})] \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{11}{6}) \\  & =\frac{11}{12}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "098028bf-3706-5127-9bb7-debd78e7b253" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408136}} {:db/id 17592186408134 :step/content {:db/id 17592186408132 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "100fac5f-cc12-56dc-9567-ee01010ba781" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186408119} {:answer/id #uuid "1377aca7-a017-58fe-8e23-256c042e11b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186408120} {:answer/id #uuid "3aabdbf2-aad9-5028-8b69-34e437771408" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{14}{15}" :db/id 17592186408121} {:answer/id #uuid "41ea5617-4c16-5bdc-a231-c9432f86dc81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{18}" :db/id 17592186408122} {:answer/id #uuid "93d7f804-0816-5794-84e7-a2fe566f8c71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{5}" :db/id 17592186408127}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186408121} :answer-field/id #uuid "85ef2574-1c06-549a-a456-4b22b82491c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186408130}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ffe5914e-4912-5ff3-9b15-3a1462960003" :question/math-academy-id "q-132285" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy\,dx=$" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type I region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy]dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}]_{{x}^{2}}^{1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-{x}^{4}-{x}^{4})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{4})\,dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=e$ intercepts the curve $y={e}^{x}$ at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$1\le x\le e.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/b7/b78021a06c9fea100b75c66a619c425345cda3666d84da018895be15a53af06d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le e,\,e\le y\le {e}^{x}}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}[{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{y\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)]}_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

double integral
${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA,$
where $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines
$x=e,$ $y=e$ and the curve $y={e}^{x}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's make a sketch of our region.

![](images/aa/aa635ca5ef3198fea56d684b034de476a72e4ace2a4c51b37c6c59977036eb76.png)

Notice that $D$ is a type I region.

- The line $y=e$ intercepts the curve $y={e}^{x}$ at $x=1.$
So, the $x$-limits are 
$1\le x\le e.$

- To determine the lower and upper functions, we draw a vertical arrow through the region.

![](images/b7/b78021a06c9fea100b75c66a619c425345cda3666d84da018895be15a53af06d.png)

As a result, the integral is defined over the following type I region: 

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le e,\,e\le y\le {e}^{x}}
$$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dA={\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{yx\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy\,dx & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}[{\int }_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\frac{1}{y\operatorname{ln}⁡y}\,dy]\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}{[\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡y)]}_{e}^{{e}^{x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡{e}^{x})-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e))\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}dx & ={[\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡x}{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡e}{2}-\frac{{ln}^{2}⁡1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "597be508-6945-5d32-9627-435849b9418f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408134}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0a7ddc79-cbfd-59b5-9638-d178b71104a6" :answer/type {:db/id :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186158396 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158469 :tutorial/content "For a $2 \times 2$ matrix differential equation

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),
$$

 

we know that if $A$ has distinct eigenvalues, the general solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{black}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{black}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

This formula works even when the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ are complex. However, using it directly requires working with complex exponentials, which can be cumbersome.

A more direct method is to find just *one* of the complex solutions, say $\mathbf x_1(t) = \mathbf{v}_1 e^{{\color{black}\lambda_1} t},$ and separate it into its *real and imaginary parts*.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t} \\  & ={{{w}_{1}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Real Part}}\,+\,\text{i}\,\,\,{{{w}_{2}(t)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Imaginary Part}}\end{aligned}
$$

The general *real-valued* solution is then a linear combination of these two parts:

$$
\mathbf x(t) = c_1 \mathbf w_1(t) + c_2 \mathbf w_2(t)
$$

**Note:** This method may seem surprising. Why can we construct the general solution using only *one* of the complex solutions, $\mathbf x_1(t)?$

The reason is that the second solution, $\mathbf x_2(t),$ doesn't provide any new information. For a real matrix $A,$ the complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors come in *conjugate pairs*, which means $\mathbf x_2(t)$ is simply the complex conjugate of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

Since $\mathbf x_2(t) = \mathbf w_1 (t) - \textrm{i} \, \mathbf w_2(t),$ it is also a linear combination of the real and imaginary parts of $\mathbf x_1(t).$

To build our general solution, we just need two *linearly independent* real solutions. The key facts are the following:

- For a system with complex eigenvalues, the real part $\mathbf w_1(t)$ and the imaginary part $\mathbf w_2(t)$ are *always* linearly independent.

- Since they are two linearly independent solutions, they can form the basis for the general solution.

So, we can use them directly and bypass the need to work with $\mathbf x_2(t)$ at all.

Let's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "a93ff6d6-1eb0-5e42-8b69-ae73fc891839" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4283 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid
