![](images/cd/cd9752c16b15ebcfcfa214c775e99fb68139a1dfa9364a5f552fbf676d7953f7.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "31f14503-26a9-5e09-b9cf-10a636f52db7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14898 :tutorial/title "Multiple Iterations of the Trapezoidal Method"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186180341} :activity/id #uuid "90074413-5fe3-5632-8eb0-3e0dc053df00" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048376 :topic/id #uuid "9a5670e8-43ef-54b7-8f4b-81842fc55f1c" :topic/math-academy-id 3715} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180341 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

![](images/63/637677324152af3d428e405c89025f35dbe5d71e2e8f0a0797ef3aca30bae7e1.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "ecd8591f-8e5b-50b2-91a1-4f15bd97b2c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9521 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1e80fc64-e097-5e8d-a35c-056416216619" :step/math-academy-id 184955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180342}} {:db/id 17592186180342 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180788 :tutorial/content "If $\mathbf{F}(x,y)$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ The symbol $\oint\limits$ means integration over the closed curve.

It's helpful to spend some time understanding where this definition comes from, so let's derive it using the closed curve $C$ below.

![](images/6d/6dfe8a071798c93f19507808596b7d32af90367b2666643d092a7c50afe5e929.png)

First, we pick a point $P$ on $C.$ At this point, we draw the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the outward-pointing normal vector $\mathbf n$ to $C.$

![](images/49/498e1afbaac8bc8297213eae09cc8bf8742b29f45dda1dfafff868c67ebb9de9.png)

We wish to calculate the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P.$ Now, $\mathbf F$ is made up of two components:

- a component parallel to $\mathbf n,$ which contributes to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ and

- a component perpendicular to $\mathbf n,$ which does *not* contribute to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$

We're only interested in the contribution made to the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C.$ This is given by the scalar projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n.$

![](images/ac/ac3aae49f372908f2f9aeb53e3fc98bff117846fca05a8c696009e443390811c.png)

Therefore, the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at $P$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{n}F & =\frac{F\cdot n}{||n||}=F\cdot n.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression above represents the flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C$ at a single point only. Therefore, to calculate the total net flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ we sum (integrate) this expression over the entire curve. This gives

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a328d4d8-bfe8-50eb-8bbd-281b3bb07afe" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9522 :tutorial/title "Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux"} :step/id #uuid "9dac0bb5-3a03-56c0-a614-dc9f045cb3e3" :step/math-academy-id 184956 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180343}} {:db/id 17592186180343 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180789 :tutorial/content "Consider the circle $S$ and vector field $\mathbf F$ below. Let $C$ be any path where $S$ is traversed once in the counterclockwise direction. 

![](images/e6/e679efaa2612d45bbfe8b918de7148853b64eaf530af34a525ef1735e0946b09.png)

By drawing an outward-pointing unit normal vector, it's clear that there is a net flow *out* through $C.$ 

![](images/fb/fbcd6fd0fadcc955212a145de9edb4654ddb92ddebb8ba31eb775cff676efeeb.png)

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$

When measuring flux through a closed curve, the curve's orientation does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same in either case. 

![](images/a3/a3d398d382e6bc94ddde77e650d50a6b5ec050083f89f64104f6f2fd172a9239.png)

So, the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $-C$ is also positive, and we have

$$
\oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s > 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "36b855d8-9994-5c22-bbc4-e28065875f84" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9523 :tutorial/title "Orientation-Independence"} :step/id #uuid "a000a04f-fdd8-5b25-9b23-e59a14a3592d" :step/math-academy-id 184957 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180344}} {:db/id 17592186180344 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179644 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179482 :question/id #uuid "c427d9b4-2944-5edc-8e19-363de348d23d" :question/math-academy-id "e-15147"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2b7b8782-d1f4-5654-a18f-6ad35de8fb30" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049212} {:db/id 17592186049653} {:db/id 17592186050104}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180031} {:db/id 17592186180032} {:db/id 17592186262687} {:db/id 17592186262688} {:db/id 17592186262690} {:db/id 17592186262691}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining a Flux's Sign From a Diagram"} :step/id #uuid "4f8760a0-8c8e-5ec6-9492-0ecc32789da6" :step/math-academy-id 184958 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180345}} {:db/id 17592186180345 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180346 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179645 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179483 :question/id #uuid "15426c37-1508-5407-ab49-b26f8761795c" :question/math-academy-id "e-15148"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9c8ca56-5ea8-547c-80ab-6b1f1347447e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180034} {:db/id 17592186180035} {:db/id 17592186235531} {:db/id 17592186262697} {:db/id 17592186262698} {:db/id 17592186262699} {:db/id 17592186262700} {:db/id 17592186262701} {:db/id 17592186362496}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Integral Expression for Flux"} :step/id #uuid "2c288a88-997c-5ef1-98ff-24092e7506f9" :step/math-academy-id 184962 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180347}} {:db/id 17592186180347 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid 17592186180787 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf F$ be a vector field on $\mathbb R^2$ and $C$ be a *closed* curve in the $xy$-plane. Imagine that $\mathbf F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and $C$ is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net). 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol C$** is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by $C.$ 

We have three possible scenarios: 

- If more water flows out through $C$ than in through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *out* through $C$), the flux is *positive*.

![](images/6f/6ff4d006d3fbf4a434f35a13c8591fc166ff6c74adf2b7969752b7541e486df2.png)

- If more water flows in through $C$ than out through $C$ (i.e., there is a net flow *in* through $C$), the flux is *negative*.

![](images/38/3812148e855a84e3233316acc8bbf59bd7cd802a874c9e4807c6efd7ca6754cf.png)

- If the net flow through $C$ is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across $C$ because the amount of water flowing in through $C$ equals the amount of water flowing out through $C.$

![](images/56/56aef4f217e9981755826745a97e8389d86b49518ffd7d3ebc75e5ee2dc28f8b.png)

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across $C$ because the water flow is tangential to $C$ at every point along $C.$

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

If $C=C_1\cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n$ is piecewise smooth, we have to calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over each smooth face. That is,

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+ \cdots +
\int\limits_{C_n} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C$ on $C_i.$

As an example, let's consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf i + (y-x)^3\,\mathbf j$ and the rectangle $C$ shown below. 

![](images/5c/5cbd62feddcce7a676a76117de09154da21abdd8b039c0e45a7a0e7d5fb00e9c.png)

To calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C,$ we sum the fluxes of $\mathbf F$ over each side:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
$$

To demonstrate how to compute these integrals, let's construct the flux integral across the side $C_4,$ given by

$$
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

The side $C_4$ and its outward-pointing unit normal are shown below.

![](images/06/06fd5a2ecbd709e8e835f2a57ef3ada772526366d51e5e16474d9b8635500e8e.png)

Since this side is perpendicular to the $y$-axis and we require an outward-pointing unit normal vector, we must have 

$$
\mathbf n = -\mathbf j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i+(y-x)^{3}\,j)\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(xy\,i)\cdot (-j)+((y-x)^{3}\,j))\cdot (-j)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}0-(y-x)^{3}\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{4}}(x-y)^{3}\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Following a similar procedure for the other sides, we can construct the full expression for the flux of $\mathbf F$ over $C.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "472c362c-27a5-5041-90c3-4533c63b736d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9524 :tutorial/title "Calculating Flux"} :step/id #uuid "ab771459-c3a6-5f4b-9e75-cfa3f13b9add" :step/math-academy-id 184961 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180346}} {:db/id 17592186180790 :tutorial/content "To calculate the flux of a vector field over a smooth, closed curve, we can use the formula

However, we can often simplify our calculations if the vector field displays symmetry.

To demonstrate, consider the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ and a square $C$ with side length $6$ centered at $O,$ as shown below. Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C.$

![](images/8e/8e1767b9bea45e742df4953f0ec50b2d43c9622994035342307dc2be6abba8de.png)

If $\mathbf{F}$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s,
$$

where the sides $C_i$ and unit vectors $\mathbf n_i$ are shown below.

![](images/65/65a8c37c64580f7d1f41f32722f20dfee2b8fd98333920a0feae781ea8d9541e.png)

Since the vector field $\mathbf F = -5\,\mathbf i$ is parallel to $C_2$ and $C_4,$ there is zero net flow through these two sides. Therefore,

$$
\int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_2 \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_4} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_4 \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$

This is easy to verify, since, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}-5\,i\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}0\,\text{d}s \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

and similarly for the integral along $C_4.$ 

So, our expression for the flux reduces to

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s
=
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+
\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s.
$$

Since the vector field is uniform, the net inflow through $C_1$ will cancel with the net outflow through $C_3.$ That is

$$
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
=
-\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_1 \: \textrm{d}s
+\int\limits_{C_3} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n}_3 \: \textrm{d}s
=0.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "53e768e4-a3bb-5b89-83b9-a97e9ff4a921" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9525 :tutorial/title "Using  Symmetry to Simplify Flux Calculations"} :step/id #uuid "5c82115b-5b07-5765-b4a2-64382478cffb" :step/math-academy-id 184965 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180348}} {:db/id 17592186180791 :tutorial/content "Calculating the flux of a vector field across a rectangle or square requires computing four flux integrals. 17592186180454}} {:db/id 17592186180453 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180703 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of *displacement.* In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.

Suppose a particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. Its displacement from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and its acceleration is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.$

![](images/52/5222b12a7f08a33dc981ac95bd717cce945e1d2e3565fb3631f108fd0f307a12.png)

Furthermore, suppose $P$ has velocity $2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $\sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.$

Let's use this information to determine at which values of $x$ the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.$$

Using the fact that $$\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),$$ we can rewrite our equation as

$$\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int 2x \:\textrm{d}x$$

which gives the general solution

$$\dfrac12v^2 = x^2+ C.$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=\sqrt 3\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}$$

Therefore,

$$\dfrac12v^2 = x^2-1.$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when $P$ is instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\,m\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dcdbb7a7-457c-5386-9a73-ae4d9da40f89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5769 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "28c57294-3b4c-56e0-8cac-331a28850e07" :step/math-academy-id 35399 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180416}} {:db/id 17592186180454 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179715 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179577 :question/id #uuid "58325462-3a69-575e-bdfb-31db815b0d3a" :question/math-academy-id "e-9456"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8c812adc-7418-5a76-9c7f-96c726c7ca0e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048478}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180095} {:db/id 17592186180096} {:db/id 17592186365253} {:db/id 17592186365260} {:db/id 17592186365281} {:db/id 17592186365288} {:db/id 17592186365302} {:db/id 17592186365309} {:db/id 17592186365316}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Maximum Speed of a Particle"} :step/id #uuid "1a2b4d25-22b2-5303-9d34-924730dd694c" :step/math-academy-id 35400}] :activity/title "Determining Properties of Objects Described as Functions of Displacement" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179847} {:db/id 17592186180453 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180703 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of *displacement.* In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.

"1a2b4d25-22b2-5303-9d34-924730dd694c" :step/math-academy-id 35400} {:db/id 17592186180703 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to calculate a particle's velocity and displacement when its acceleration is a function of *displacement.* In this lesson, we'll use this knowledge to compute various properties of a particle in motion.

Suppose a particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. Its displacement from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and its acceleration is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2.$

![](images/52/5222b12a7f08a33dc981ac95bd717cce945e1d2e3565fb3631f108fd0f307a12.png)

Furthermore, suppose $P$ has velocity $2\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $\sqrt{3}\,\rm{m}.$

Let's use this information to determine at which values of $x$ the particle is instantaneously at rest.

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2x\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2x.$$

Using the fact that $$\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),$$ we can rewrite our equation as

$$\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x.$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x} \left(\dfrac12v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int 2x \:\textrm{d}x$$

which gives the general solution

$$\dfrac12v^2 = x^2+ C.$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=\sqrt 3\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =(\sqrt{3})^{2}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1\end{aligned}$$

Therefore,

$$\dfrac12v^2 = x^2-1.$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x) = 0\,\rm{m/s}.$ We find the displacement of the particle when $P$ is instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x{:}$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-1 \\ {x}^{2} & =1 \\ x & =\pm 1\,m\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dcdbb7a7-457c-5386-9a73-ae4d9da40f89" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5769 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186167843} :activity/id #uuid "be95ee71-ebc4-546c-a738-6a6db824342c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048395 :topic/id #uuid "9bb55214-36f6-5124-91d2-24ff1cb653aa" :topic/math-academy-id 3242} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167843 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167997 :tutorial/content "Consider a *decoupled* linear system of ODEs

Recall that the eigenvalues for a diagonal matrix are its diagonal entries, ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/af/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) 
The corresponding eigenvectors are parallel to the coordinate axes:

Notice that if a solution starts on one of the coordinate axes, it remains on that axis. These are called **straight-line solutions**:

The stability of these solutions as ![](images/91/919e9a7f2e074404c564846d6d8e1576e63b42ecbcc768b97d0632c645e32f22.svg) depends on the *signs* of the eigenvalues ![](images/77/77bce8fda831b5be2b2f52e043375447e794f8dad01a666d45e08716e912d707.svg) and ![](images/af/afb536c2c395100d85543d9c25f58d867e0bcfbd5f826d794284b648e7cc0550.svg) We will explore the three main stability cases in the upcoming examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "3ab2b715-abcc-511c-bbda-a2664d39efda" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14436 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a60bbebf-7d50-57b0-b823-f5cde68f6ecb" :step/math-academy-id 588112 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167852}} {:db/id 17592186167844 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168002 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0.$ 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/75/75e7a0e16141db2a8da210c1ab30fc7328ccc98f861afec4db69d951ff3c9121.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/28/280e99a308962d43d1060be7100e294623d3bc3bfbe0579ab61d817695ad9e45.svg) Since $\lambda_2>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *away* from the origin (*unstable axis*).

Because both axes are *unstable*, the origin (equilibrium point) is called an **unstable node** or **source**.

In the phase portrait, we draw:

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), and

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin).

A typical trajectory for an *unstable node* emanates from the origin toward infinity.

To do this, we can compare the rates of change of ![](images/f7/f7dbfa03976240534a1b57f2cc59c474401a0d9524bc5f627736da01a0d775c1.svg) and ![](images/cc/cc436bde605f3822acb66d36528ba42a812a50fdbea361b31f0dbd0cba61d810.svg) by looking at the slope of the tangent line to the trajectory, ![](images/c7/c7244a31f756199a29c0e7e755eccdf9274346e643e0856566469b35a207e53a.svg) Assuming ![](images/37/371aec72d3e326e3e52fbd1a1cfc06be06b33e3054e60b8c286a9fcbac39141e.svg) we have:

As we can see, the long-term behavior of the slope as ![](images/91/919e9a7f2e074404c564846d6d8e1576e63b42ecbcc768b97d0632c645e32f22.svg) depends on the sign of the exponent, ![](images/7c/7cde6653feb562f0d136150bffa6f2925af0c7dbcb9ede5c7f1b3e0f10f3796d.svg)

This comparison is governed by which eigenvalue is larger. We call the larger eigenvalue (the one that is more positive, or less negative) the **dominant eigenvalue**.

In the next slides, we will analyze the source and sink cases separately." :tutorial/id #uuid "406ac21a-bfe3-5af2-bc34-8bb09ae11870" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14456 :tutorial/title "Dominant Eigenvalue"} :step/id #uuid "7d22549d-343c-5238-823d-0fdd3d6b11cf" :step/math-academy-id 588121 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167960}} {:db/id 17592186167849 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166914 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166542 :question/id #uuid "74560a13-4a23-553d-8c8d-6c040f03a957" :question/math-academy-id "e-21633"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1c5ee85e-c6ce-5c8e-bb14-d0a32d6810e4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049543} {:db/id 17592186050531}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167207} {:db/id 17592186167235} {:db/id 17592186308404} {:db/id 17592186308405} {:db/id 17592186391057} {:db/id 17592186391144} {:db/id 17592186391151} {:db/id 17592186420023} {:db/id 17592186420026}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Phase Portrait Given a System: Advanced Cases"} :step/id #uuid "edbdd357-26e5-5671-9724-72c90fe9512d" :step/math-academy-id 588122 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167850}} {:db/id 17592186167850 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168004 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fd81402-072b-5676-9cac-f53af20f3174" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14462 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b8abcadd-58fc-5f3e-a1a9-f6f32aaa7405" :step/math-academy-id 588125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167851}} {:db/id 17592186167851 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166915 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166540 :question/id #uuid "4926ad20-fc6b-5a7d-80ee-aa39421c174d" :question/math-academy-id "e-21607"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "24bd917d-c4b3-5bf5-9426-a87a579b03c1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167200} {:db/id 17592186167236} {:db/id 17592186308409} {:db/id 17592186308410} {:db/id 17592186308411} {:db/id 17592186391158} {:db/id 17592186391169} {:db/id 17592186420019} {:db/id 17592186420021} {:db/id 17592186420025}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Decoupled Systems of Linear Differential Equations"} :step/id #uuid "6cadc020-1f0c-5e3d-88b7-c3977e63cc74" :step/math-academy-id 588126} {:db/id 17592186167852 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168020 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a decoupled system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

Again, we are considering a decoupled linear system
![](images/e1/e1efdd0b8c037c01450042384ce3bac663d0b549fa9557d0db09b692754cab0f.svg)

Recall that a homogeneous linear system has a single equilibrium point at the origin $(0,0).$ 
To classify this equilibrium, we look at the signs of $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2.$

First of all, the coordinate axes are straight-line solutions:

- On the $x$-axis, we have $y(t)= 0$ and $x(t)=c_1e^{\lambda_1 t}$.

- If $\lambda_1<0,$ the $x$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- *Unstable node (source)* if $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2>0.$

- *Stable node (sink)* if $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2<0.$ In fact, it's asymptotically stable, as the trajectories converge to the origin.

- *Saddle point* if $\lambda_1\lambda_2<0$ (one positive, one negative).

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "6fd81402-072b-5676-9cac-f53af20f3174" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14462 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "b8abcadd-58fc-5f3e-a1a9-f6f32aaa7405" :step/math-academy-id 588125 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167851}} {:db/id 17592186168004 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

- If $\lambda_1>0,$ the $x$-axis is an *unstable* line.

- On the $y$-axis, we have $x(t)=0$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{\lambda_2 t}.$

- If $\lambda_2<0,$ the $y$-axis is a *stable* line.

- If $\lambda_2>0,$ the $y$-axis is an *unstable* line.

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{1}x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where $\lambda_1>0$ and $\lambda_2<0$ (the opposite case, where $\lambda_1<0$ and $\lambda_2>0,$ is similar). 

Let's now determine the behavior along the axes.

- The straight-line solutions on the $x$-axis have the form ![](images/4d/4dc3aaf0f7dfd85070df84c13abe2cf02d85a704167569b3d3a76f2b58178c5b.svg) Since $\lambda_1>0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_1 t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $x$-axis move *away* from the origin. This is called an **unstable axis**.

- The straight-line solutions on the $y$-axis have the form ![](images/76/76f6b9bbcdff2c87295fb0cd14dbdbbaa5e6c75eeb49c1cc158a4e8bd3da059d.svg) Since $\lambda_2<0,$ we have that $e^{\lambda_2 t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the trajectories on the $y$-axis move *toward* the origin. This is called a **stable axis**.

Because one axis is stable and the other is unstable, the origin (equilibrium point) is called a **saddle point**.

In the phase portrait, we draw

- arrows on the $x$-axis pointing *outward* (away from the origin), while

- arrows on the $y$-axis pointing *inward* (toward the origin).

A typical trajectory bends from the stable direction and then peels away along the unstable direction.

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

It is common for the set $S$ of a continuous random variable $X$ to be an infinite interval. Therefore, we often need to evaluate improper integrals when determining whether a function is a valid pdf and to compute probabilities associated with such a random variable.

For example, let's consider the following function:

![](images/38/38ea105f5dd0cea7784bf73f814e7161b90cfd224eb099084cc33b6539d95fdd.svg)

Is $f(x)$ a valid probability density function? Let's start by sketching its graph:

![](images/35/3559a998491a004c159683aaf0946bb4fdf87f4afe873fdc93235e840b4b0ac8.png)

Clearly, $f(x)\geq 0$ for all $x,$ so this function satisfies the first condition.

To check that $f(x)$ satisfies the second condition, we need to compute the following integral:

$$
\int_S f(x)\,\textrm d x = \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,\textrm d x
$$

Calculating this integral using the usual methods, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x & ={[-{e}^{-x}]}_{0}^{\infty } \\  & =[-{e}^{-\infty }]-[-{e}^{0}] \\  & =0-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $f(x)$ satisfies both conditions, we conclude that $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "f9c0835e-afeb-5f5c-b296-1e37ad68d3fa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6775 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :step/math-academy-id 32202} {:db/id 17592186172929 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173171 :tutorial/content "A very important (although very hard to prove) result in mathematics states the following:

Any simple and closed curve divides the plane into exactly two regions, one inside the curve and one outside.

Based on this fact, we can define the **orientation** of a simple closed curve as follows:

A simple closed curve is **positively oriented** if, when traveling along it, one always has the curve interior to the left and the curve exterior to the right. Otherwise, the curve is **negatively oriented**.

For example, curve I shown below is positively oriented, while curve II is negatively oriented:

![](images/95/9527dd8bdfd979a1d521ccf945e84ef9b557d67e3d89ce8f5e4f7bb8d287ee8c.png)

An alternative convenient way of looking at simple oriented curves is that a curve is positively oriented if it is traversed *counterclockwise* and it is negatively oriented if it is traversed *clockwise*." :tutorial/id #uuid "4c2c2591-a914-53a3-9f60-6e7335d049f4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5165 :tutorial/title "Oriented Curves"} :step/id #uuid "2b76b9e7-6d5f-584c-837f-bd003bd3c835" :step/math-academy-id 32465 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172918}}] :activity/title "Simple, Closed, and Oriented Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186172178} {:db/id 17592186172909 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173163 :tutorial/content "A  plane curve

:tutorial/content "For a first-order initial value problem, we have already seen ways to approximate the increment in $y$ over a step, including:

- the modified Euler method, which predicts using Euler's method and then corrects that prediction, and

- the RK4 method, which combines several slope evaluations within a single step.

Another group of methods, called the **Adams-Bashforth-Moulton methods**, takes a different approach. Rather than computing multiple slopes at new points, these methods reuse slopes from previous steps in a predictor-corrector framework, giving high accuracy with relatively little additional work.

In this lesson, we'll focus on one of the simplest: the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method. For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c,
$$

the predictor equation of the **$2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method** (**ABM $2$-step**) with step size $\Delta x$ is

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1}) \cdot \Delta x,
$$

where

- $y' = f(x,y)$ is the slope at the current point $(x,y),$ and

- $y'_{-1} = f(x_{-1}, y_{-1})$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}),$ where $x_{-1} = x-\Delta x.$

The initially predicted new $y$-value is then given by $y_p = y + \Delta y_p.$

Since ABM $2$-step uses the slope from the previous step, it cannot be started from a single initial condition alone. 
Instead, we initialize the method by computing the first step with a one-step method, typically the RK4 method.

Once the prediction $y_p$ is computed, we apply a corrector equation to refine our approximation. We'll return to this step shortly.
Before that, let's see an example of how to apply the predictor equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "50a2f37b-38d8-5a6f-bc13-9086af674ed7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14412 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5af445aa-9ec9-5489-9176-c4332bff0a03" :step/math-academy-id 611738 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222407}} {:db/id 17592186222407 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222510 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 4x - 2y, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$

Let's begin the process of applying the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method to approximate the value of $y(1).$

We know $y(0)$ and wish to estimate $y(1).$ Since the method takes $2$ steps (one to initialize, one to approximate), we will use a step size of

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{1-0}2 = \dfrac12.
$$

We will use a table to keep track of known values. First, we add the initial condition data:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

Next, we initialize the ABM $2$-step method by making a preliminary step with a one-step method.

Applying the RK4 method with step size $\Delta x = \dfrac12,$ we obtain the slope $y'=-2,$ increment $\Delta y = -\dfrac14,$ and approximation

$$
y\left(\dfrac12\right)\approx 1 + \left(-\dfrac14\right) = \dfrac34.
$$

We add the slope to the table, and the approximation in a new row.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |  |  |

Note that, since RK4 is not a predictor-corrector method, there is no increment $\Delta y_p$ or predictor $y_p$ for this step. So, we leave these entries in the first row blank.

Now, we continue from this point, using the ABM $2$-step method.
First, we compute the value of $y'$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =4x-2y \\  & =4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-2\cdot (\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ |  |  |

From the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Next, we compute $\Delta y_p$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{7}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ |  |

Hence, according to the predictor equation, the initially predicted new $y$-value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{8} \\  & =\frac{13}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed table is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |

Therefore, our initial prediction for $y(1)$ is $y_p = \dfrac{13}8.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3c403981-071d-5b27-8ff8-99c1ea98715b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14615 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "fb2bf195-d713-5c11-b38c-0b93be4ea2b8" :step/math-academy-id 611739 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222408}} {:db/id 17592186222408 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221458 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221161 :question/id #uuid "c736760f-414e-5ab2-adfa-c09acce10d5e" :question/math-academy-id "e-21539"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "874de02f-c5be-54ed-8d66-a3b1f1f23c9a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049048} {:db/id 17592186050891}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221937} {:db/id 17592186221958} {:db/id 17592186308367} {:db/id 17592186308372} {:db/id 17592186308373}] :knowledge-point/title "Completing a Table Using the Predictor Equation of the ABM 2-Step Method"} :step/id #uuid "183435e5-3131-5485-8b09-dfbc5b6bc6b9" :step/math-academy-id 611740 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222409}} {:db/id 17592186222409 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222479 :tutorial/content "For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c,
$$

the **$2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton** (**ABM $2$-step**) **Method** with step size $\Delta x$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx, \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx,\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $y' = f(x,y)$ is the estimated slope at the current point $(x,y),$

- $y'_{-1} = f(x_{-1}, y_{-1})$ is the estimated slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}),$ and

- $y'_p = f(x_\text{new}, y_p)$ is the estimated slope at the predicted new point $(x_\text{new}, y_p) = (x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y_p).$

The final approximation for the new step is $y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y.$

So, the corrector of the ABM $2$-step combines the slope evaluated at the predicted point with the slope evaluated at the current point and the previous point. Let's demonstrate how to apply the corrector equation to our previous example." :tutorial/id #uuid "684ff8c6-ca91-5e58-82e6-41d645b1e6db" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14372 :tutorial/title "The Two-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method"} :step/id #uuid "78553a6e-4fa7-55a6-9f7b-b53ad1a3a237" :step/math-academy-id 611743 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222410}} {:db/id 17592186222410 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222480 :tutorial/content "Let's return to the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 4x-2y, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$

We will now complete our approximation of the value of $y(1)$ using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method.

First, recall that we previously initialized with the RK4 method and completed the predictor step of the ABM $2$-step method, resulting in the following values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |  |  |

Now, the slope at the point $(x_\text{new},y_p) = \left(\dfrac12+\dfrac12, \dfrac{13}8\right) = \left(1, \dfrac{13}8\right)$ estimated by the predictor is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{'} & =4{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p} \\  & =4\cdot 1-2\cdot \frac{13}{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |

Looking at the partially filled table, we note the following:

- From the second row, the slope at the current point $(x, y) = \left(\dfrac12, \dfrac34\right)$ is $y' = \dfrac12.$

- From the first row, the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Finally, we compute $\Delta y$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot \frac{3}{4}+8\cdot \frac{1}{2}-(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}\cdot \frac{39}{4} \\  & =\frac{13}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed row is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac{13}{32}$ |

We know the value of $x$ in the next row is $x_\text{new}=1.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $\Delta y$ to $y{:}$

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y = \dfrac34 + \dfrac{13}{32} = \dfrac{37}{32}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac{13}{32}$ |
| $1$ | $\dfrac{37}{32}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1) \approx \dfrac{37}{32}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "098a5bb7-0ece-59ec-8400-a8e3efe1b00a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14385 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid 17592186308417} {:db/id 17592186308418} {:db/id 17592186308421} {:db/id 17592186308446} {:db/id 17592186308447} {:db/id 17592186308448} {:db/id 17592186374686} {:db/id 17592186374711}] :question/math-academy-id "e-21566"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5a37e3d-f1ce-57f2-baef-c464a4f89ad4" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221934} {:db/id 17592186221979} {:db/id the Solution to an Initial Value Problem Using The ABM 2-Step Method"} :step/id #uuid "40865e2e-2c40-5544-acb9-196c8c726a9f" :step/math-academy-id 611751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222414}} {:db/id 17592186222414 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222485 :tutorial/content "Where do the predictor and corrector equations of the two-step Adams–Bashforth–Moulton method come from?

The method consists of two parts: the **Adams-Bashforth** (**AB2**) **predictor**, and **Adams-Moulton** (**AM2**) **corrector**.
We'll begin by deriving the AB2 predictor.

Consider an initial value problem:

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a)=c
$$

Writing the differential equation in integral form, we have

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Let $\Delta x = x_\text{new} - x$ be the step size, and define the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t - x}{\Delta x}.
$$

Then, $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so the integral becomes

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x.
$$

Now, define a new function $g$ of $\theta$ as the integrand:

$$
g(\theta) = f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))
$$

The Adams formulas result from approximating $g(\theta)$ by a simple function that agrees with its known values, and then integrating that approximation from $0$ to $1.$ We now determine some known values.

- Evaluating $g$ at $\theta = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(0) & =f(x+0\cdot Δx,y(x+0\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x,y) \\  & ={y}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, evaluating $g$ at $\theta=-1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =f(x+(-1)\cdot Δx,y(x+(-1)\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x-Δx,y(x-Δx)) \\  & =f({x}_{-1},y({x}_{-1})) \\  & ={y}_{-1}^{'},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_{-1}$ is the previous $x$-value and $y'_{-1}$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).$

Since we have two known values, the simplest reasonable approximation to $g(\theta)$ is a *straight line* passing through these two points: $(0,y')$ and $(-1,y'_{-1}).$
This straight line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\theta ) & ={y}^{'}+\frac{{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}}{0-(-1)}(\theta -0) \\  & ={y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by integrating this approximation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta )\,d\theta  \\  & ={({y}^{'}\theta +\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}){\theta }^{2})|}_{\theta \,=\,0}^{\theta \,=\,1} \\  & ={y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy={\int }_{0}^{1}g(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx\approx {\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx=\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

It is this approximation that we define as the AB2 predictor:

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

The Adams formulae result from approximating [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a polynomial interpolant constructed from known function values and integrating that polynomial from [math]0[/math] to [math]1.[/math]

Notice that evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta = 0,[/math] we have
\begin{align*}
g(0) &= f(x + 0\cdot\Delta x, y(x + 0\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x, y) \\[5pt]
&= y'.
\end{align*}

Similarly, evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta=-1[/math], we get
\begin{align*}
g(-1)
&= f(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x, y(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x - \Delta x, y(x - \Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})) \\[5pt]
&= y'_{-1},
\end{align*}

where [math]y'_{-1}[/math] is the slope at the previous point [math](x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).[/math]
So, to derive the AB2 predictor, we can approximate [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a *linear* interpolant using its values at [math]\theta=0[/math] and [math]\theta=-1.[/math]

The Lagrange basis polynomials are
\[
\ell_0(\theta) = \theta + 1,\qquad
\ell_{-1}(\theta) = -\theta,
\]

so the interpolant is
\begin{align*}
p(\theta) &= g(0)\ell_0(\theta) - g(-1)\ell_{-1}(\theta) \\[5pt]
&= y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta.
\end{align*}

Finally, by integrating the interpolant, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta
&= \int_0^1 \big(y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta\big) \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\int_0^1 (\theta + 1) \,\mathrm{d}\theta - y'_{-1} \int_0^1 \theta \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\left[\dfrac12\theta^2 + \theta\right]_0^1 - y'_{-1}\left[\dfrac12\theta^2\right]_0^1 \\[5pt]
&= y'\left(\dfrac12 + 1 - 0\right) - y'_{-1}\left(\dfrac12 - 0\right) \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the AB2 predictor is
\begin{align*}
\Delta y \approx \Delta y_p &= \int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \left(\dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}\right)\cdot\Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "dee56e00-8f80-598d-a5ea-b99a6322bddd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14478 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AB2 Predictor"} :step/id #uuid "d6baca6f-a078-54e6-b8c4-a3e52eb82476" :step/math-academy-id 611754 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222415}} {:db/id 17592186222415 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222486 :tutorial/content "So far, we have derived the AB2 predictor. We are left to derive the AM2 corrector.

Recall that we wrote the differential equation in integral form as

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

With the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t-x}{\Delta x},
$$

we had $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,
$$

and we defined

$$
g(\theta) = f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x)).
$$

For the predictor, we considered two known values of $g(\theta){:}$ 

- For $\theta = 0,$ we have $g(0) = y'.$

- For $\theta = -1,$ we have $g(-1) = y'_{-1}.$

Then, we approximated $g$ with a linear function passing through these two points.

Now, for the corrector, we use *three* known values, and approximate $g(\theta)$ by a *quadratic* passing through these three points.

To obtain a third value, we also want the slope at the *new* $x$-value $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x.$ But, the true value $y_\text{new}$ is not yet known.

Instead, we evaluate the slope at the new point estimated by the AB2 predictor! This corresponds to $\theta = 1{:}$

$$
g(1) = f(x + \Delta x, y(x + \Delta x)) \approx f(x_\text{new}, y_p) = y'_p,
$$

where $y_p$ is the new $y$-value predicted by AB2, and $y'_p$ is the slope evaluated at $(x_\text{new}, y_p).$
So, our three points are

$$
(-1,y'_{-1}), \quad (0,y'), \quad (1,y'_p).
$$

Let $q(\theta)$ be the quadratic that passes through these three points. After simplifying, this quadratic can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\theta ) & =\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta +1){y}_{p}^{'}-(\theta -1)(\theta +1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta -1){y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate this approximation from $0$ to $1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}q(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'})\,d\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}){y}_{p}^{'}-(\frac{1}{3}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}){y}_{-1}^{'}-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{12}{y}_{p}^{'}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{'}-\frac{1}{12}{y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 g(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
\approx \int_0^1 q(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
= \dfrac1{12}(5y'_p + 8y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

It is this approximation that we use as the AM2 corrector. Putting it together, the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5aa97723-f737-5f47-be29-c04919e09c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14479 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AM2 Corrector"} :step/id #uuid "5990a7fa-57e1-5d5e-9ae3-587f865f923b" :step/math-academy-id 611755}] :activity/title "The ABM2 Method" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221477} {:db/id 17592186222406 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222483 :tutorial/content "For a first-order initial value problem, we have already seen ways to approximate the increment in $y$ over a step, including:

- the modified Euler method, which predicts using Euler's method and then corrects that prediction, and

- the RK4 method, which combines several slope evaluations within a single step.

Another group of methods, called the **Adams-Bashforth-Moulton methods**, takes a different approach. Rather than computing multiple slopes at new points, these methods reuse slopes from previous steps in a predictor-corrector framework, giving high accuracy with relatively little additional work.

In this lesson, we'll focus on one of the simplest: the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method. For an initial value problem

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a) = c,
$$

the predictor equation of the **$2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method** (**ABM $2$-step**) with step size $\Delta x$ is

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1}) \cdot \Delta x,
$$

where

- $y' = f(x,y)$ is the slope at the current point $(x,y),$ and

- $y'_{-1} = f(x_{-1}, y_{-1})$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}),$ where $x_{-1} = x-\Delta x.$

The initially predicted new $y$-value is then given by $y_p = y + \Delta y_p.$

Since ABM $2$-step uses the slope from the previous step, it cannot be started from a single initial condition alone. 
Instead, we initialize the method by computing the first step with a one-step method, typically the RK4 method.

Once the prediction $y_p$ is computed, we apply a corrector equation to refine our approximation. We'll return to this step shortly.
Before that, let's see an example of how to apply the predictor equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "50a2f37b-38d8-5a6f-bc13-9086af674ed7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14412 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "5af445aa-9ec9-5489-9176-c4332bff0a03" :step/math-academy-id 611738 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222407}} {:db/id 17592186222483 :tutorial/content "For a first-order initial value problem, we have already seen ways to approximate the increment in $y$ over a step, including:

In this lesson, we'll focus on one of the simplest: the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method. For an initial value problem

the predictor equation of the **$2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method** (**ABM $2$-step**) with step size $\Delta x$ is

$$

$$

where

- $y' = f(x,y)$ is the slope at the current point $(x,y),$ and

Once the prediction $y_p$ is computed, we apply a corrector equation to refine our approximation. We'll return to this step shortly.
Before that, let's see an example of how to apply the predictor equation." :tutorial/id #uuid "50a2f37b-38d8-5a6f-bc13-9086af674ed7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14412 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222407 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222510 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 4x - 2y, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$

Let's begin the process of applying the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method to approximate the value of $y(1).$

We know $y(0)$ and wish to estimate $y(1).$ Since the method takes $2$ steps (one to initialize, one to approximate), we will use a step size of

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{1-0}2 = \dfrac12.
$$

We will use a table to keep track of known values. First, we add the initial condition data:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ |  |  |  |

Next, we initialize the ABM $2$-step method by making a preliminary step with a one-step method.

Applying the RK4 method with step size $\Delta x = \dfrac12,$ we obtain the slope $y'=-2,$ increment $\Delta y = -\dfrac14,$ and approximation

$$
y\left(\dfrac12\right)\approx 1 + \left(-\dfrac14\right) = \dfrac34.
$$

We add the slope to the table, and the approximation in a new row.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |  |  |

Note that, since RK4 is not a predictor-corrector method, there is no increment $\Delta y_p$ or predictor $y_p$ for this step. So, we leave these entries in the first row blank.

Now, we continue from this point, using the ABM $2$-step method.
First, we compute the value of $y'$ according to the given rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{'} & =4x-2y \\  & =4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-2\cdot (\frac{3}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ |  |  |

From the table, we see that the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Next, we compute $\Delta y_p$ using the predictor equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\cdot (\frac{1}{2})-(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{7}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

We add this value to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ |  |

Hence, according to the predictor equation, the initially predicted new $y$-value is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =y+Δ{y}_{p} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}+\frac{7}{8} \\  & =\frac{13}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed table is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |

Therefore, our initial prediction for $y(1)$ is $y_p = \dfrac{13}8.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3c403981-071d-5b27-8ff8-99c1ea98715b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14615 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "fb2bf195-d713-5c11-b38c-0b93be4ea2b8" :step/math-academy-id 611739 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222408}} {:db/id 17592186222510 :tutorial/content "Consider the following initial value problem:

the **$2$-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton** (**ABM $2$-step**) **Method** with step size $\Delta x$ is given by

Let's demonstrate how to apply the corrector equation to our previous example." :tutorial/id #uuid "684ff8c6-ca91-5e58-82e6-41d645b1e6db" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14372 :tutorial/title "The Two-Step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method"} {:db/id 17592186222410 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222480 :tutorial/content "Let's return to the following initial value problem:

$$
y' = 4x-2y, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$

We will now complete our approximation of the value of $y(1)$ using the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method.

First, recall that we previously initialized with the RK4 method and completed the predictor step of the ABM $2$-step method, resulting in the following values:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ |  |  |

Now, the slope at the point $(x_\text{new},y_p) = \left(\dfrac12+\dfrac12, \dfrac{13}8\right) = \left(1, \dfrac{13}8\right)$ estimated by the predictor is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{'} & =4{x}_{\text{new}}-2{y}_{p} \\  & =4\cdot 1-2\cdot \frac{13}{8} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can add this to our table.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ |  |

Looking at the partially filled table, we note the following:

- From the second row, the slope at the current point $(x, y) = \left(\dfrac12, \dfrac34\right)$ is $y' = \dfrac12.$

- From the first row, the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y_{-1}) = \left(0, 1\right)$ is $y'_{-1} = -2.$

Finally, we compute $\Delta y$ using the corrector equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5\cdot \frac{3}{4}+8\cdot \frac{1}{2}-(-2))\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}\cdot \frac{39}{4} \\  & =\frac{13}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the completed row is as given below.

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac{13}{32}$ |

We know the value of $x$ in the next row is $x_\text{new}=1.$ To get the value of $y$ in the next row, we add $\Delta y$ to $y{:}$

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \Delta y = \dfrac34 + \dfrac{13}{32} = \dfrac{37}{32}
$$

Adding these results to our table gives the following:

| $\,x\,$ | $\,y\,$ | $\,y'\,$ | $\Delta y_p$ | $y_p$ | $y'_p$ | $\Delta y$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $1$ | $-2$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-$ | $-\dfrac{1}{4}$ |
| $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac78$ | $\dfrac{13}8$ | $\dfrac34$ | $\dfrac{13}{32}$ |
| $1$ | $\dfrac{37}{32}$ |  |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we conclude that $y(1) \approx \dfrac{37}{32}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "098a5bb7-0ece-59ec-8400-a8e3efe1b00a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14385 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "702af9a1-f869-585a-9d62-8b4e15161407" :step/math-academy-id 611744 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222411}} {:db/id 17592186222480 :tutorial/content "Let's return to the following initial value problem:

predictor and corrector equations of the two-step Adams–Bashforth–Moulton method come from?

The method consists of two parts: the **Adams-Bashforth** (**AB2**) **predictor**, and **Adams-Moulton** (**AM2**) **corrector**.
We'll begin by deriving the AB2 predictor.

Consider an initial value problem:

$$
y' = f(x,y), \qquad y(a)=c
$$

Writing the differential equation in integral form, we have

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_{x}^{x_\text{new}} f(t, y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Let $\Delta x = x_\text{new} - x$ be the step size, and define the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t - x}{\Delta x}.
$$

Then, $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so the integral becomes

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x.
$$

Now, define a new function $g$ of $\theta$ as the integrand:

$$
g(\theta) = f(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x, y(x + \theta\cdot\Delta x))
$$

The Adams formulas result from approximating $g(\theta)$ by a simple function that agrees with its known values, and then integrating that approximation from $0$ to $1.$ We now determine some known values.

- Evaluating $g$ at $\theta = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}g(0) & =f(x+0\cdot Δx,y(x+0\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x,y) \\  & ={y}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, evaluating $g$ at $\theta=-1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-1) & =f(x+(-1)\cdot Δx,y(x+(-1)\cdot Δx)) \\  & =f(x-Δx,y(x-Δx)) \\  & =f({x}_{-1},y({x}_{-1})) \\  & ={y}_{-1}^{'},\end{aligned}
$$

where $x_{-1}$ is the previous $x$-value and $y'_{-1}$ is the slope at the previous point $(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).$

Since we have two known values, the simplest reasonable approximation to $g(\theta)$ is a *straight line* passing through these two points: $(0,y')$ and $(-1,y'_{-1}).$
This straight line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\theta ) & ={y}^{'}+\frac{{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}}{0-(-1)}(\theta -0) \\  & ={y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by integrating this approximation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{'}+({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\theta )\,d\theta  \\  & ={({y}^{'}\theta +\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}){\theta }^{2})|}_{\theta \,=\,0}^{\theta \,=\,1} \\  & ={y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy={\int }_{0}^{1}g(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx\approx {\int }_{0}^{1}p(\theta )\,d\theta \cdot Δx=\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx.\end{aligned}
$$

It is this approximation that we define as the AB2 predictor:

$$
\Delta y_p = \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

The Adams formulae result from approximating [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a polynomial interpolant constructed from known function values and integrating that polynomial from [math]0[/math] to [math]1.[/math]

Notice that evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta = 0,[/math] we have
\begin{align*}
g(0) &= f(x + 0\cdot\Delta x, y(x + 0\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x, y) \\[5pt]
&= y'.
\end{align*}

Similarly, evaluating [math]g[/math] at [math]\theta=-1[/math], we get
\begin{align*}
g(-1)
&= f(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x, y(x + (-1)\cdot\Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x - \Delta x, y(x - \Delta x)) \\[5pt]
&= f(x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})) \\[5pt]
&= y'_{-1},
\end{align*}

where [math]y'_{-1}[/math] is the slope at the previous point [math](x_{-1}, y(x_{-1})).[/math]
So, to derive the AB2 predictor, we can approximate [math]g(\theta)[/math] by a *linear* interpolant using its values at [math]\theta=0[/math] and [math]\theta=-1.[/math]

The Lagrange basis polynomials are
\[
\ell_0(\theta) = \theta + 1,\qquad
\ell_{-1}(\theta) = -\theta,
\]

so the interpolant is
\begin{align*}
p(\theta) &= g(0)\ell_0(\theta) - g(-1)\ell_{-1}(\theta) \\[5pt]
&= y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta.
\end{align*}

Finally, by integrating the interpolant, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta
&= \int_0^1 \big(y'\cdot(\theta + 1) - y'_{-1}\cdot\theta\big) \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\int_0^1 (\theta + 1) \,\mathrm{d}\theta - y'_{-1} \int_0^1 \theta \,\mathrm{d}\theta \\[5pt]
&= y'\left[\dfrac12\theta^2 + \theta\right]_0^1 - y'_{-1}\left[\dfrac12\theta^2\right]_0^1 \\[5pt]
&= y'\left(\dfrac12 + 1 - 0\right) - y'_{-1}\left(\dfrac12 - 0\right) \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, the AB2 predictor is
\begin{align*}
\Delta y \approx \Delta y_p &= \int_0^1 p(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \left(\dfrac32y' - \dfrac12y'_{-1}\right)\cdot\Delta x \\[5pt]
&= \dfrac12(3y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
\end{align*}" :tutorial/id #uuid "dee56e00-8f80-598d-a5ea-b99a6322bddd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14478 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AB2 Predictor"} :step/id #uuid "d6baca6f-a078-54e6-b8c4-a3e52eb82476" :step/math-academy-id 611754 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222415}} {:db/id 17592186222485 :tutorial/content "Where do the predictor and corrector equations of the two-step Adams–Bashforth–Moulton method come from?

We are left to derive the AM2 corrector.

Recall that we wrote the differential equation in integral form as

$$
y_\text{new} = y + \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta y = \int_x^{x_\text{new}} f(t,y(t))\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

With the change of variables

$$
\theta = \dfrac{t-x}{\Delta x},
$$

we had $t = x + \theta\cdot\Delta x$ and $\mathrm{d}t = \mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,$ so

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x))\,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x,
$$

and we defined

$$
g(\theta) = f(x+\theta\Delta x,y(x+\theta\Delta x)).
$$

For the predictor, we considered two known values of $g(\theta){:}$ 

- For $\theta = 0,$ we have $g(0) = y'.$

- For $\theta = -1,$ we have $g(-1) = y'_{-1}.$

Then, we approximated $g$ with a linear function passing through these two points.

Now, for the corrector, we use *three* known values, and approximate $g(\theta)$ by a *quadratic* passing through these three points.

To obtain a third value, we also want the slope at the *new* $x$-value $x_\text{new} = x + \Delta x.$ But, the true value $y_\text{new}$ is not yet known.

Instead, we evaluate the slope at the new point estimated by the AB2 predictor! This corresponds to $\theta = 1{:}$

$$
g(1) = f(x + \Delta x, y(x + \Delta x)) \approx f(x_\text{new}, y_p) = y'_p,
$$

where $y_p$ is the new $y$-value predicted by AB2, and $y'_p$ is the slope evaluated at $(x_\text{new}, y_p).$
So, our three points are

$$
(-1,y'_{-1}), \quad (0,y'), \quad (1,y'_p).
$$

Let $q(\theta)$ be the quadratic that passes through these three points. After simplifying, this quadratic can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\theta ) & =\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta +1){y}_{p}^{'}-(\theta -1)(\theta +1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}\theta (\theta -1){y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate this approximation from $0$ to $1{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}q(\theta )\,d\theta  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}+\theta ){y}_{p}^{'}-({\theta }^{2}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}({\theta }^{2}-\theta ){y}_{-1}^{'})\,d\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}){y}_{p}^{'}-(\frac{1}{3}-1){y}^{'}+\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}){y}_{-1}^{'}-0 \\  & =\frac{5}{12}{y}_{p}^{'}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{'}-\frac{1}{12}{y}_{-1}^{'} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the approximation of the increment in $y$ is

$$
\Delta y = \int_0^1 g(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
\approx \int_0^1 q(\theta) \,\mathrm{d}\theta\cdot\Delta x
= \dfrac1{12}(5y'_p + 8y' - y'_{-1})\cdot\Delta x.
$$

It is this approximation that we use as the AM2 corrector. Putting it together, the $2$-step Adams-Bashforth-Moulton method is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Predictor} & : & Δ{y}_{p} & =\frac{1}{2}(3{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx \\ \text{Corrector} & : & Δy & =\frac{1}{12}(5{y}_{p}^{'}+8{y}^{'}-{y}_{-1}^{'})\cdot Δx\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5aa97723-f737-5f47-be29-c04919e09c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14479 :tutorial/title "Derivation of the AM2 Corrector"} :step/id #uuid "5990a7fa-57e1-5d5e-9ae3-587f865f923b" :step/math-academy-id 611755} {:db/id 17592186222486 :tutorial/content "So far, we have derived the AB2 predictor. $$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r .
$$

This integral represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from an initial point $A$ to a terminal point $B$ along the curve.

If the curve can be parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then we can calculate the line integral using the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r= \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt
$$

Often, the trickiest part is finding a parameterization for $C.$ In this lesson, we'll consider several different cases" :tutorial/id #uuid "ec010a30-571c-5ad5-b30a-c18ffdd997e1" :step/content {:db/id 17592186180718 :tutorial/content "The line integral of a vector-valued function $\mathbf F$ along a piecewise smooth curve $C$ is denoted

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r .
$$

This integral represents the total work done by $\mathbf F$ in moving a particle from an initial point $A$ to a terminal point $B$ along the curve.

If the curve can be parameterized by the function $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ then we can calculate the line integral using the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d\mathbf r= \int_a^b \mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) \cdot \mathbf r'(t)\,\textrm dt
$$

Often, the trickiest part is finding a parameterization for $C.$ In this lesson, we'll consider several different cases" :tutorial/id #uuid "ec010a30-571c-5ad5-b30a-c18ffdd997e1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5823 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7b85eebf-c70c-58a0-9476-5bcb73727ad3" :step/math-academy-id 35690 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180491}} {:db/id 17592186180718 :tutorial/content "The line integral of a vector-valued function $\mathbf F$ along a piecewise smooth curve $C$ is denoted
